stimuli.title: Twelve persons in two facing rows of six
stimuli.content:
Twelve persons Arya, Bhola, Chanda, Dhiren, Gulab, Hasan, Kapil, Lalit, Mohan, Nayan, Ravi and Tulsi sit in two parallel rows of six seats each. The persons in Row 1 face south and those in Row 2 face north, so each person faces exactly one person of the other row. (Facing south, the right is towards the west; facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Mohan sits in Row 1, third from the east end of that row.
- Hasan faces Mohan, and Bhola sits immediately to the right of Hasan.
- Tulsi sits immediately to the right of Mohan, and Dhiren faces Tulsi.
- Ravi sits second to the left of Mohan, and Gulab sits between Mohan and Ravi.
- Lalit faces Ravi, and Chanda sits at one end of Row 2.
- Nayan faces Arya, who sits in the row that faces south.
stimuli.solution:
Number the columns 1 to 6 from the west in both rows.
Step 1: Mohan = Row 1, column 4. Hasan faces him: Row 2, column 4; Bhola, to Hasan's right (east): Row 2, column 5.
Step 2: Tulsi, to Mohan's right (west): Row 1, column 3; Dhiren faces her: Row 2, column 3.
Step 3: Ravi, second to Mohan's left (east): Row 1, column 6; Gulab between them: column 5. Lalit faces Ravi: Row 2, column 6, so Chanda is at the other end: Row 2, column 1.
Step 4: Free seats: Row 1 columns 1 and 2, Row 2 column 2. Nayan faces Arya, so they take the facing pair Row 2 column 2 and Row 1 column 2; Arya is in the south-facing Row 1, so Nayan is in Row 2, and Kapil gets Row 1, column 1.

| Column | Row 1 (facing south) | Row 2 (facing north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kapil | Chanda |
| 2 | Arya | Nayan |
| 3 | Tulsi | Dhiren |
| 4 | Mohan | Hasan |
| 5 | Gulab | Bhola |
| 6 | Ravi | Lalit |

stimuli.title: Ten seats, seven persons
stimuli.content:
Ten seats are placed in a straight row and numbered 1 to 10 from the left end. Seven persons Anvi, Bhim, Chiru, Dolu, Esha, Fuzail and Gita sit on seven of them, all facing north; the other three seats are vacant. Positions such as 'second to the right' count seats, including vacant ones.

- Anvi sits on seat 6, and Chiru sits immediately to the right of Anvi.
- Bhim sits at the extreme left end, and Dolu at the extreme right end.
- Fuzail sits immediately to the left of Dolu.
- Esha and Gita sit in adjacent seats, Esha to the left of Gita, and exactly one seat lies between Bhim and Esha.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Anvi = 6, Chiru = 7, Bhim = 1, Dolu = 10, Fuzail = 9.
Step 2: One seat lies between Bhim (1) and Esha: Esha = 3, and Gita, immediately to her right, = 4.
Step 3: The vacant seats are 2, 5 and 8.

| Seat | Person |
|---|---|
| 1 | Bhim |
| 2 | vacant |
| 3 | Esha |
| 4 | Gita |
| 5 | vacant |
| 6 | Anvi |
| 7 | Chiru |
| 8 | vacant |
| 9 | Fuzail |

stimuli.title: Eight persons in a row, ranked by height
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Hiran, Ishu, Kuku, Lado, Mitu, Nanki, Pammi and Rinku sit in a straight row, all facing north. No two of them are of the same height. (Facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Lado and Pammi sit at the two ends of the row, Lado at the left end.
- The tallest person sits immediately to the right of Lado, and the shortest person sits immediately to the right of the tallest person.
- Nanki is the second tallest and sits second to the right of the tallest person.
- Hiran sits second to the right of Nanki and is shorter than only Kuku and Nanki.
- Kuku is taller than Nanki.
- Ishu sits immediately to the left of Hiran, and Rinku immediately to the right of Hiran.
- Ishu is shorter than everyone except the shortest person; Rinku is taller than Lado, and Lado is taller than Pammi.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 8 from the left.
Step 1: Lado = 1, Pammi = 8. The tallest person is on seat 2 and the shortest on seat 3. Nanki (2nd tallest) = 4, Hiran (3rd tallest) = 6, Ishu = 5, Rinku = 7.
Step 2: Kuku and Mitu take seats 2 and 3. Kuku is taller than Nanki, the second tallest, so Kuku is the tallest (seat 2) and Mitu the shortest (seat 3).
Step 3: Ranks 4 to 7 remain for Ishu, Rinku, Lado and Pammi. Ishu is 7th; Rinku > Lado > Pammi in height: Rinku 4th, Lado 5th, Pammi 6th.

| Seat | Person | Height rank |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lado | 5 |
| 2 | Kuku | 1 |
| 3 | Mitu | 8 |
| 4 | Nanki | 2 |
| 5 | Ishu | 7 |
| 6 | Hiran | 3 |
| 7 | Rinku | 4 |
| 8 | Pammi | 6 |

stimuli.title: Ten chairs, eight persons
stimuli.content:
Ten chairs are placed around a circular table, equally spaced. Eight persons Ajay, Bimal, Disha, Fateh, Jassi, Lucky, Rupal and Ujjal sit on eight of them, all facing the centre; two chairs are vacant. Positions such as 'second to the right' count chairs, including vacant ones. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise.)

- Jassi sits opposite Ajay, and Bimal sits immediately to the left of Jassi.
- Rupal sits immediately to the right of Ajay. Fateh sits second to the right of Rupal, and the chair between Rupal and Fateh is vacant.
- Lucky sits immediately to the left of Ajay, and Disha sits immediately to the left of Lucky.
- Ujjal sits immediately to the right of Jassi.
- The two vacant chairs are exactly opposite each other.
stimuli.solution:
Number the chairs 0 to 9 anticlockwise from Ajay.
Step 1: Jassi = 5 (opposite), Bimal = 4 (Jassi's left, clockwise), Ujjal = 6.
Step 2: Rupal = 1, chair 2 is vacant, Fateh = 3.
Step 3: Lucky = 9, Disha = 8. The only chair left is 7, which is vacant — and it is exactly opposite chair 2, as required.

| Chair | Person |
|---|---|
| 0 | Ajay |
| 1 | Rupal |
| 2 | vacant |
| 3 | Fateh |
| 4 | Bimal |
| 5 | Jassi |
| 6 | Ujjal |
| 7 | vacant |
| 8 | Disha |
| 9 | Lucky |

stimuli.title: Seven persons facing in or out
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Rohit, Saloni, Tanuj, Urvi, Vedika, Xena and Yuvi sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some of them face the centre and the others face outside. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)

- Rohit faces the centre, and Urvi sits immediately to his right.
- Urvi faces outside, and Yuvi sits immediately to Urvi's left.
- Saloni sits immediately to the right of Yuvi, and the two of them face opposite directions.
- Vedika sits immediately to the left of Rohit and faces the same direction as Rohit.
- Tanuj sits immediately to the left of Vedika.
- Xena faces the centre, Xena and Tanuj face opposite directions, and Yuvi faces the same direction as Xena.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 6 anticlockwise from Rohit.
Step 1: Rohit faces the centre: Urvi = 1. Urvi faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Yuvi = 2.
Step 2: Vedika, on Rohit's left (clockwise), = 6 and faces the centre. Tanuj, on Vedika's left, = 5.
Step 3: Xena faces the centre; Yuvi faces the same way (centre), Tanuj the other way (outside). Saloni faces opposite to Yuvi (outside) and sits on Yuvi's right (anticlockwise): 3. Xena takes seat 4.

| Seat | Person | Facing |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Rohit | facing the centre |
| 1 | Urvi | facing outside |
| 2 | Yuvi | facing the centre |
| 3 | Saloni | facing outside |
| 4 | Xena | facing the centre |
| 5 | Tanuj | facing outside |
| 6 | Vedika | facing the centre |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six hobbies
stimuli.content:
Six persons Bablu, Chameli, Dinu, Ganesh, Heena and Jagan live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 6 the topmost). Each has a different hobby among Dancing, Painting, Reading, Singing, Swimming and Writing.

- Chameli lives on floor 4, Bablu immediately above her and Jagan immediately below her.
- Dinu lives on the topmost floor, and Heena lives below Ganesh.
- The person who likes Painting lives on an even-numbered floor between Jagan and Bablu.
- The person on the topmost floor likes Singing, and the person on floor 1 likes Reading.
- The person who likes Dancing lives immediately below the person who likes Painting.
- Bablu does not like Swimming.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Chameli = 4, Bablu = 5, Jagan = 3, Dinu = 6. Floors 1 and 2 remain; Heena is below Ganesh: Heena = 1, Ganesh = 2.
Step 2: Painting is on an even floor between 3 and 5: floor 4 (Chameli). Dancing is immediately below: floor 3 (Jagan). Singing: floor 6 (Dinu). Reading: floor 1 (Heena).
Step 3: Swimming and Writing remain for Ganesh and Bablu; Bablu does not swim: Bablu Writing, Ganesh Swimming.

| Floor | Person | Hobby |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Dinu | Singing |
| 5 | Bablu | Writing |
| 4 | Chameli | Painting |
| 3 | Jagan | Dancing |
| 2 | Ganesh | Swimming |
| 1 | Heena | Reading |

stimuli.title: Two persons on each of four floors, with colours
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Arif, Chinki, Gudiya, Hanif, Lalu, Mamta, Pintu and Sweety live in a four-storey building, two persons on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 4 the topmost). Each likes a different colour among Amber, Coral, Indigo, Lilac, Mint, Navy, Rose and Tan.

- Gudiya lives on floor 3 and likes Rose.
- Arif lives on the floor immediately above Gudiya's and likes Mint.
- Hanif lives on an even-numbered floor below Gudiya.
- Chinki and Mamta live on the same floor.
- Sweety lives above Lalu, and Pintu lives on the floor immediately below Lalu's.
- The person who likes Navy lives on the topmost floor. Hanif likes Amber and Pintu likes Lilac.
- The person who likes Tan lives on floor 3, and Chinki does not like Indigo.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gudiya = 3 (Rose), Arif = 4 (Mint), Hanif = 2 (Amber).
Step 2: Chinki and Mamta share a floor; floors 2, 3 and 4 each have only one free place, so they live on floor 1.
Step 3: Lalu, Pintu and Sweety fill one place each on floors 2, 3 and 4. Pintu is immediately below Lalu and Sweety is above Lalu: Pintu = 2, Lalu = 3, Sweety = 4.
Step 4: Navy is on floor 4; Arif likes Mint, so Sweety likes Navy. Pintu likes Lilac. Tan is on floor 3, where Gudiya likes Rose, so Lalu likes Tan. Coral and Indigo remain for Chinki and Mamta; Chinki does not like Indigo: Chinki Coral, Mamta Indigo.

| Floor | Persons (colour) |
|---|---|
| 4 | Arif (Mint), Sweety (Navy) |
| 3 | Gudiya (Rose), Lalu (Tan) |
| 2 | Hanif (Amber), Pintu (Lilac) |
| 1 | Chinki (Coral), Mamta (Indigo) |

stimuli.title: A basement, a ground floor and six floors
stimuli.content:
A building has a basement, a ground floor and six floors above the ground floor (floors 1 to 6, floor 6 being the topmost). Eight persons Abhi, Barun, Chaya, Dilip, Emily, Feroz, Gagan and Harsha live in it, one on each of these eight levels. Each has a different profession among Actor, Baker, Cashier, Doctor, Editor, Farmer, Guard and Nurse. 'Level' means any of the eight (basement, ground floor or floor 1-6).

- Exactly three persons live above Emily, and Emily is the Actor.
- The Doctor lives two levels below Emily.
- Chaya lives on the ground floor, immediately above the Guard.
- Barun lives on the topmost floor, and Dilip lives two levels below Barun.
- Gagan lives between Dilip and Barun.
- Feroz lives below Harsha, and Abhi lives immediately above Harsha.
- The Nurse lives immediately above the Doctor.
- The Cashier lives immediately below the Editor, and the Editor lives below the Farmer.
stimuli.solution:
List the levels from the bottom: basement, ground, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Step 1: Three persons live above Emily, so Emily is on floor 3 (the Actor). The Doctor is two levels lower: floor 1.
Step 2: Chaya = ground floor; the Guard is in the basement. Barun = floor 6, Dilip = floor 4, Gagan = floor 5.
Step 3: Feroz, Harsha and Abhi take the basement, floor 1 and floor 2. Abhi is immediately above Harsha and Feroz below Harsha: Feroz = basement (Guard), Harsha = floor 1 (Doctor), Abhi = floor 2.
Step 4: The Nurse is immediately above the Doctor: Abhi. Baker, Cashier, Editor and Farmer remain for Chaya (ground), Dilip (4), Gagan (5) and Barun (6). Cashier is immediately below Editor, and Editor is below Farmer: Cashier 4 (Dilip), Editor 5 (Gagan), Farmer 6 (Barun). Chaya is the Baker.

| Level | Person | Profession |
|---|---|---|
| floor 6 | Barun | Farmer |
| floor 5 | Gagan | Editor |
| floor 4 | Dilip | Cashier |
| floor 3 | Emily | Actor |
| floor 2 | Abhi | Nurse |
| floor 1 | Harsha | Doctor |
| the ground floor | Chaya | Baker |
| the basement | Feroz | Guard |

stimuli.title: Eight coloured boxes in a stack
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes A, C, E, H, K, N, R and W are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 8 the top). Each box is of a different colour among Aqua, Black, Cyan, Gold, Ivory, Lime, Plum and Rust.

- Box A is kept fourth from the bottom and is Black; Box N is kept immediately above Box A.
- Box K is kept at the top, and Box H is kept immediately below Box K.
- Box C is kept between Box N and Box H, and Box R is kept at the bottom.
- Box W is kept above Box E.
- The Ivory box is kept immediately above the Black box, and the top box is Cyan.
- The Gold box is kept two places below the Black box, and the Plum box is kept between the Gold and Black boxes.
- The Rust box is kept immediately below the Cyan box, and the bottom box is not Aqua.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: A = 4 (Black), N = 5, K = 8, H = 7, C = 6, R = 1.
Step 2: Positions 2 and 3 remain for E and W; W is above E: E = 2, W = 3.
Step 3: Ivory = 5 (N), Cyan = 8 (K), Gold = 2 (E), Plum = 3 (W), Rust = 7 (H).
Step 4: Aqua and Lime remain for R (1) and C (6); the bottom box is not Aqua: R Lime, C Aqua.

| Position | Box | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | K | Cyan |
| 7 | H | Rust |
| 6 | C | Aqua |
| 5 | N | Ivory |
| 4 | A | Black |
| 3 | W | Plum |
| 2 | E | Gold |
| 1 | R | Lime |

stimuli.title: Eight boxes on two shelves
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes B, D, F, H, J, L, N and P are placed on two shelves, upper and lower, four boxes on each shelf in a line. Each box on the upper shelf is directly above one box on the lower shelf. Left and right are as seen from the front.

- Box J is on the upper shelf, third from the left, and Box F is directly below Box J.
- Box L is immediately to the right of Box F, and Box B is directly above Box L.
- Box H is at the left end of the lower shelf, and Box P is on the lower shelf.
- Box D is directly above Box P.
stimuli.solution:
Number the places 1 to 4 from the left on each shelf.
Step 1: J = upper 3, F = lower 3, L = lower 4, B = upper 4.
Step 2: H = lower 1. P is on the lower shelf: the only free place there is 2. D is directly above P: upper 2.
Step 3: N takes the last place, upper 1.

| Shelf | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upper | N | D | J | B |
| Lower | H | P | F | L |

stimuli.title: Seven boxes of three sizes
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes C, G, M, Q, T, V and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom). Three boxes are Large, two Medium and two Small.

- No box is kept directly on top of a box smaller than itself.
- Box Y is Medium, and Box C is kept immediately below Box Y.
- Box M is kept at the top, and Box T is Small.
- Box G is kept immediately below Box T.
- Box V is kept below Box Q.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: No box sits on a smaller box, so sizes never increase going up: positions 1–3 are Large, 4–5 Medium and 6–7 Small.
Step 2: M = 7 (Small). T is Small: T = 6, and G, immediately below T, = 5 (Medium).
Step 3: Y is Medium: the only Medium place left is 4, so Y = 4 and C = 3 (Large).
Step 4: V and Q take 1 and 2 with V below: V = 1, Q = 2.

| Position | Box | Size |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | M | Small |
| 6 | T | Small |
| 5 | G | Medium |
| 4 | Y | Medium |
| 3 | C | Large |
| 2 | Q | Large |
| 1 | V | Large |

stimuli.title: Five filled and hollow shapes for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, five shapes are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A ◆ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ◇ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A ▼ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ▽ B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A ○ B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ◆ means >, ◇ means ≥, ▼ means <, ▽ means ≤ and ○ means =. Rewrite the statements with ordinary signs, join them into a chain and test each conclusion.

stimuli.title: Five children and their chocolates
stimuli.content:
Five children Golu, Hiya, Jojo, Kiku and Lalli have different numbers of chocolates.

- Hiya has more chocolates than Golu but fewer than Kiku.
- Jojo has fewer chocolates than Golu.
- Lalli has more chocolates than Kiku.
stimuli.solution: Golu < Hiya < Kiku < Lalli, and Jojo < Golu. Order (most first): Lalli, Kiku, Hiya, Golu, Jojo.

stimuli.title: Six school posts and six subjects
stimuli.content:
Six teachers Kamini, Lokesh, Madhav, Naina, Oorja and Pratik of a school hold six different posts. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: Principal, Vice-Principal, Coordinator, Senior Teacher, Teacher and Assistant Teacher. Each teaches a different subject among Maths, Science, English, History, Art and Music.

- The Maths teacher is senior to exactly four of the others.
- The History teacher is the Principal.
- Kamini is junior to the Maths teacher but senior to Pratik.
- Lokesh is the most junior, and he teaches neither Music nor Art.
- Pratik teaches Science, and Naina teaches Music and is junior to Pratik.
- Madhav is senior to Oorja.
- The Art teacher is senior to the Science teacher.
stimuli.solution:
The Maths teacher has four people below: Vice-Principal. The Principal teaches History. Lokesh is the Assistant Teacher (rank 6). Pratik teaches Science and Naina Music, Naina junior to Pratik; Kamini is junior to the Vice-Principal but senior to Pratik. So Kamini > Pratik > Naina > Lokesh fills ranks 3 to 6: Kamini Coordinator, Pratik Senior Teacher, Naina Teacher. Madhav and Oorja take ranks 1 and 2, Madhav senior: Madhav Principal (History), Oorja Vice-Principal (Maths). Lokesh teaches neither Music nor Art, so English; Kamini teaches Art (and is senior to the Science teacher, as required).

Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Assistant Teacher–English.

stimuli.title: Three symbol codes for relations
stimuli.solution: Decode pair by pair from the left; the parents of a child are a married couple.

stimuli.title: A family described in three codes
stimuli.content:
In a certain code, 'A ⊕ B' means 'A is a parent of B', 'A ⊗ B' means 'A is married to B' and 'A ⊖ B' means 'A and B are siblings'. Kartik, Mehul, Pranav and Qasim are male; Leela, Naina, Ojasvi and Riya are female. The following are true:

- Kartik ⊗ Leela
- Leela ⊕ Mehul
- Mehul ⊖ Naina
- Ojasvi ⊗ Mehul
- Ojasvi ⊕ Pranav
- Qasim ⊗ Naina
- Qasim ⊕ Riya
stimuli.solution:
Leela, Kartik's wife, is a parent of Mehul, and Naina is Mehul's sibling, so both are children of Kartik and Leela. Ojasvi is Mehul's wife and Pranav's mother; Qasim is Naina's husband and Riya's parent.
Tree: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya.

stimuli.title: A taxi's route with five stops
stimuli.content: A taxi leaves its depot D and drives in straight lines: 6 km east to stop A, then 8 km north to stop B, then 12 km west to stop C, then 5 km south to stop E, and finally 10 km east to stop F, where it ends its trip.
stimuli.solution: With D at (0, 0), east and north positive: A (6, 0), B (6, 8), C (−6, 8), E (−6, 3), F (4, 3).

stimuli.title: Six points with a midpoint
stimuli.content:
Six points J, K, L, M, N and O lie on flat ground.

- J is 10 m east of K.
- L is 10 m north of J.
- M is the midpoint of the straight line joining K and L.
- N is 5 m south of M.
- O is 7 m west of M.

stimuli.title: A three-part code that depends on word length
stimuli.content:
In a certain code, a word is written as: its last letter, then the number of letters in the word, then the letter that comes two places after its first letter in the English alphabet. If the word has an even number of letters, the whole code is then written in reverse order.
For example, TRAIN is written as N5V and HOME is written as J4E.
stimuli.solution: Odd length: last letter + length + (first letter + 2). Even length: the same three parts, reversed.

stimuli.title: Arrangement of 17 elements beginning with W

stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a row, all facing north.

- Arun is 8th from the left end.
- Bela sits to the right of Arun, and exactly five persons sit between Arun and Bela.
- Chetan sits third to the left of Bela.

stimuli.title: A pinch of iodine
stimuli.content:
For most of us, salt is just salt: something we add to food without a second thought. Yet the packet in an Indian kitchen today usually carries a small word printed on it: 'iodised'. Behind that word lies one of the cheapest and most successful public health measures ever attempted.

The human body needs only a tiny amount of iodine, but it cannot do without it. The thyroid gland in the neck uses iodine to make hormones that control growth and the development of the brain. When the diet lacks iodine, the gland swells, producing a visible lump in the neck known as goitre. The hidden damage is worse. A mother who lacks iodine during pregnancy may give birth to a child whose mental development is permanently held back.

Iodine deficiency is common in hilly regions and in areas prone to floods, where rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil. Crops grown in such soil contain little of it, and so do the people who eat them. For generations, whole villages in the Himalayan foothills were known for the number of people with swollen necks.

The solution that health experts settled on was simple. Instead of asking people to change their diet, they decided to add a little iodine to something everybody already eats every day. Salt was the ideal choice. Rich and poor alike consume it, in roughly similar amounts, and adding iodine to it costs only a few paise per kilogram. India launched a national programme against goitre in the 1960s, and over the following decades iodised salt became the norm in most households.

The work is not finished, however. Some families still buy cheap loose salt from small producers who do not add iodine to it. Iodine can also be lost from salt that is stored carelessly. Damp air, heat and sunlight all cause it to escape, so a packet left open near the stove may slowly lose much of its value.

The advice to households is therefore easy to follow: buy salt that is labelled 'iodised' and keep it in a closed, dry container away from the stove. It is a small habit, but it protects the most valuable thing a child carries into the world: a healthy mind.

stimuli.title: Money nobody claims
stimuli.content:
Somewhere in the records of almost every Indian bank lies money that nobody seems to own. A savings account opened for a scholarship and then forgotten, a fixed deposit made by a grandfather who never told anyone about it, a salary account left behind when its holder moved to another city: such balances add up, across the country, to many thousands of crores of rupees.

Money becomes unclaimed for ordinary reasons. People change jobs and towns and open new accounts without closing the old ones. Small balances seem too trivial to bother about. Most often, an account holder dies and the family simply does not know that the account exists. The passbook may lie in a trunk for years, or there may be no passbook at all.

Banks do not keep this money for themselves. When an account has seen no transaction by its holder for a long time, the bank marks it as inactive and tries to reach the customer. If the deposit remains unclaimed for ten years, the bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India. The money still belongs to the depositor. If the rightful owner or the legal heirs come forward, even many years later, the bank must pay it back.

Claiming it, however, can be a tiring process. Heirs who were never named in the bank's records may have to produce a death certificate, proof of their relationship and sometimes papers from a court, which can take months to obtain.

Much of this trouble can be avoided by one simple step: nomination. When opening an account or making a deposit, a customer can name a person, the nominee, to whom the bank will pay the money after the customer's death. Where a nominee is registered, the bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork. Yet many people leave the nomination form blank, either because they do not understand it or because they find it uncomfortable to think about death.

The Reserve Bank has also set up a website on which people can search for unclaimed deposits held in their own names or in the names of family members. Still, the surest protection lies at home: keep a list of all your accounts, tell your family where the list is kept, and register a nominee for every one of them.

stimuli.title: What seventy per cent means
stimuli.content:
When the weather report says that there is a seventy per cent chance of rain tomorrow, what exactly is it promising? Surveys in several countries have found that people read such forecasts in surprisingly different ways. Some believe that it will rain for seventy per cent of the day. Others think that rain will fall over seventy per cent of the area. A good number simply round the figure up and treat it as a promise of rain.

None of these readings is correct. The figure means that, at any given spot in the forecast area, there is a seven-in-ten chance of at least some measurable rain during the period. Put another way, if the same forecast were issued on a hundred days with similar conditions, rain would be expected on about seventy of them, and on the other thirty it would stay dry.

Where does such a number come from? The atmosphere is so sensitive that a tiny error in today's measurements can grow into a large error in tomorrow's forecast. Forecasters therefore often run their computer models many times, each time starting from slightly different conditions. If most of these runs produce rain at a place, the chance of rain there is high; if only a few do, it is low.

This has an uncomfortable consequence for forecasters. A dry day after a forecast of seventy per cent does not prove that the forecast was wrong; three days in ten are expected to be dry. Yet people tend to remember such days as failures. The fair way to judge a forecaster is over many forecasts: of all the days for which she predicted a seventy per cent chance, did it actually rain on roughly seventy per cent? A forecaster whose figures pass this test is said to be well calibrated, even if she is sometimes 'wrong' on a particular day.

A probability is also more useful than a plain yes or no, because different people can act on it differently. A family planning an outdoor wedding, for whom rain would be a disaster, may hire a tent even when the chance is only thirty per cent. A farmer deciding whether to spray his crop, which a shower would wash off, may wait unless the chance is very low. The same forecast, rightly understood, leads sensible people to different decisions.

stimuli.title: Why the work always takes longer
stimuli.content:
Almost everyone has had the experience. A report that was supposed to take a weekend takes a fortnight; a kitchen that was to be rebuilt in a month is still full of dust after three. Large projects show the same pattern on a grander scale. Flyovers, metro lines and new airports routinely open years after their promised dates and at costs well above their original budgets.

Psychologists have a name for this tendency: the planning fallacy. It describes our habit of underestimating how long our own tasks will take, even when we know that similar tasks in the past took longer than planned. In one well-known study, students were asked to estimate when they would finish their final-year thesis, and also to give a 'worst-case' estimate in case everything went badly. On average, they took longer than even their worst-case estimate.

Why do people who are otherwise sensible keep making the same mistake? Part of the answer lies in how we plan. When we think about a task, we picture the particular steps it requires and imagine them going roughly as intended. This is called taking the 'inside view'. What we leave out are the many things that are not part of the plan at all: an illness, a delayed supplier, a sudden demand from the boss. Each of these is unlikely on its own, but over a long project it is almost certain that some of them will happen.

Memory makes matters worse. When a past project overran, we tend to explain the delay as a special case (the rains came early, a key worker resigned) rather than as a sign of how projects usually go. Having explained the delay away, we expect the next project to run smoothly.

The most effective remedy is to take the 'outside view'. Instead of starting from the details of the plan, a planner first asks how long similar projects actually took, and then adjusts that figure for anything that makes the present case genuinely different. Some governments now require planners of large public works to compare their estimates with the record of comparable projects before a budget is approved.

Curiously, people are often better at predicting how long other people's tasks will take than their own. Asked about a colleague's project, we naturally think of the colleague's past record; asked about our own, we think of our plan. The best forecast for one's own work may come from imagining that it belongs to someone else.

stimuli.title: The pull of the average
stimuli.content:
Many years ago, a psychologist was telling a group of flight instructors that praise teaches better than punishment. One of the instructors objected. In his experience, he said, when he praised a trainee pilot for an unusually smooth landing, the next landing was usually worse; when he shouted at a trainee after a rough one, the next was usually better. Praise, he concluded, made pilots careless, and criticism made them try harder.

His observation was accurate, but his conclusion was not. Any skill performed again and again varies from one attempt to the next. Part of the variation reflects real ability, and part is simply luck: a gust of wind, a moment's distraction. An unusually good landing is likely to have been helped by good luck as well as skill, and luck does not repeat on demand. The next landing will therefore tend to be closer to the trainee's normal standard, that is, worse, whatever the instructor says. In the same way, an unusually bad landing is likely to be followed by a better one. Statisticians call this pattern regression to the mean.

The instructor had been fooled because his words always came at the extremes. He praised only after the best landings and shouted only after the worst, so the natural movement back towards the average looked like the effect of his words.

The same trap appears in many places. Patients tend to visit a doctor when their symptoms are at their worst, and many would improve in the following days even if they did nothing; whatever remedy they took gets the credit. A school that gives extra coaching to the students who did worst in one test will usually find that their next scores rise, even if the coaching is useless. A city that installs speed cameras at the junctions with the most accidents last year will probably see accidents there fall, partly because last year's figures were unusually high.

None of this means that coaching, medicines or speed cameras do not work. It means that a simple before-and-after comparison cannot tell us whether they do. To judge the true effect, we need a comparison group: similar patients who did not take the remedy, or similar junctions, chosen in the same way, where no cameras were installed. Only the difference between the two groups shows what the measure itself achieved.

stimuli.title: A positive result
stimuli.content:
Suppose a disease affects one person in every thousand, and a screening test for it is quite accurate: it correctly detects 99 of every 100 people who have the disease, but it also wrongly flags 5 of every 100 healthy people. A man takes the test and the result is positive. How worried should he be?

Most people, including many doctors when they are asked such questions, guess that he very probably has the disease, perhaps with a chance of 95 per cent. The real answer is surprisingly different. Imagine that 1,00,000 people are tested. About 100 of them have the disease, and the test flags 99 of these. Of the remaining 99,900 healthy people, 5 in every 100, or 4,995, are also flagged. Altogether, 5,094 people test positive, and only 99 of them are actually ill. A positive result therefore means a chance of fewer than 2 in 100 that the man has the disease.

The mistake people make is to ignore how rare the disease is to begin with, a figure statisticians call the base rate. Because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones, even a small error rate among the healthy produces far more false alarms than there are true cases. The test's accuracy, quoted on its own, hides this.

This does not make screening useless. A positive result raises the man's chance of being ill from 1 in 1,000 to nearly 2 in 100, a nearly twenty-fold increase, which is good reason for a second, more precise test. What it does mean is that the first result should be treated as a reason for further checks, not as a diagnosis. It also explains why doctors are often cautious about testing large numbers of people for rare conditions: the anxiety, cost and sometimes risky follow-up procedures suffered by the many healthy people who are wrongly flagged can outweigh the benefit to the few who are truly ill.

The same reasoning applies far beyond medicine. A fraud-detection system at a bank, an airport scanner or any filter that hunts for rare problems among millions of ordinary cases will, unless it is extraordinarily precise, raise far more false alarms than real ones.

stimuli.title: Twenty seconds at the tap
stimuli.content:
Washing hands with soap is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy. Doctors say that the habit can (1) ______ many common illnesses, such as diarrhoea and colds, which spread when germs travel from dirty hands to the mouth, nose or eyes.

Many people believe that rinsing their hands with water is enough. It is not. Germs (2) ______ to the natural oils on our skin, and water alone slides over these oils without removing them. Soap breaks up the oil, so that the germs can be washed away.

How we wash also matters. Hands should be rubbed together with soap for at least twenty seconds, which is about as long as it takes to hum a short song twice. The backs of the hands, the spaces between the fingers and the area under the nails are easily (3) ______, and germs often hide there.

The most important moments to wash are before eating, before cooking or feeding a child, and after using the toilet. Health workers in many villages now teach children to (4) ______ these moments with simple rhymes and with pictures painted on school walls.

Some schools have gone further. They have built long rows of taps near the dining area, so that a whole class can wash at once before the midday meal. Teachers report that children who once (5) ______ the task now rush to the taps, and that fewer pupils stay at home because of stomach infections.

The habit costs very little. A bar of soap is cheap, and where running water is not (6) ______, a simple tap made from a hanging plastic bottle can be enough. It is hard to think of any other medicine that does so much good for so little money.

stimuli.title: One clock for a wide country
stimuli.content:
All of India runs on a single clock. Indian Standard Time, five and a half hours ahead of Greenwich, is based on a line of longitude that (1) ______ near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, roughly in the middle of the country. Whether one lives in Kutch or in Arunachal Pradesh, the clock on the wall shows the same time.

The country, however, is wide. From its western edge to its eastern edge it stretches across nearly thirty degrees of longitude, and the sun rises almost two hours earlier in the far east than in the far west. In the north-east, summer dawn can break before four in the morning, and by the time offices and schools open by the clock, several hours of daylight have already been (2) ______. In the evening, the sun sets early, and homes and offices must switch on their lights, which adds to the demand for electricity.

For this reason, there have long been calls for a second time zone for the north-eastern states. Supporters point out that the tea gardens of Assam have, since colonial days, followed their own local clock, set about an hour ahead of Indian Standard Time, so that work can begin soon after sunrise. They argue that a separate zone would let people make better use of daylight and would (3) ______ electricity.

Opponents are not convinced. They fear that two time zones would cause confusion in railway and airline timetables, where a mistake about the time can have serious (4) ______. Some also argue that a single clock is a symbol of national unity.

Between these positions lies a middle course that has attracted growing attention: keep one time zone, but allow states in the east to (5) ______ their office and school hours, opening and closing earlier than the rest of the country. Such a change would capture much of the benefit of a new zone without redrawing the national clock.

stimuli.title: The tub nobody buys
stimuli.content:
A cinema sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub for ₹150 and a large one for ₹300. Most customers, unwilling to pay double, choose the small tub. Then the cinema adds a third option, a medium tub for ₹280. Hardly anyone buys it, yet sales of the large tub **(1) plummet**.

The medium tub, it turns out, was never meant to be sold. Its job is to make the large tub look like a bargain: for only twenty rupees more than the medium, the customer gets far more popcorn. Marketers call such an option a decoy, and the pattern it creates is known as the decoy effect. The decoy works because people rarely judge prices in **(2) isolation**. Faced with a single price, most of us have little idea whether it is fair. Faced with two options that are easy to compare, we seize on the comparison and let it guide the choice. The decoy is therefore designed to be clearly **(3) superior** to the option the seller wants to sell, yet only slightly cheaper than it, so that the target option wins the comparison.

Subscription offers often use the same trick. A magazine that offers a digital edition for ₹1,000 a year, a print edition for ₹2,500, and print and digital together, also for ₹2,500, is not being generous by **(4) accident**. Few readers want the print edition alone, but its presence makes the combined offer look like a free gift, and the combined offer is what the publisher hoped to sell all along.

Critics argue that decoys **(5) honour** a quirk of the mind rather than serve the customer. Defenders reply that no one is forced to buy anything, and that the decoy merely highlights a deal that genuinely is good value. The truth probably lies between the two. A decoy does not deceive in the way a false label does; every price on the board is real. But it does **(6) steer** choices in a direction the seller has chosen, and a buyer who knows the trick is better placed to ask a simple question: would I still want this option if the decoy were not there?

stimuli.title: Status word of a note-sorting machine
stimuli.content:
A currency note-sorting machine in a cash-processing centre reports its state to the controller as one 16-bit status word, shown in hexadecimal. The bits are numbered 15 (leftmost) to 0 (rightmost):

| Bits | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 15-13 | Mode | 3-bit operating mode |
| 12-5 | Count | 8-bit unsigned number of notes in the current bundle |
| 4-0 | Error | 5-bit error code |

The status word received at 10:42 is **9C5A** (hexadecimal).
stimuli.solution: 9C5A = 1001 1100 0101 1010 in binary. Mode = bits 15-13 = 100 = 4; Count = bits 12-5 = 1110 0010 = 226; Error = bits 4-0 = 11010 = 26. As an unsigned number the word is 40,026, which is 116132 in octal. Rotating the word left by 4 bits moves the leading hex digit 9 to the end: C5A9.

stimuli.title: Program on a teaching accumulator processor
stimuli.content:
A bank's IT training lab uses a simple processor with one register for data, the accumulator (ACC), and a program counter (PC) that always holds the address of the NEXT instruction to fetch. Each instruction occupies one memory word and is fetched with ONE memory access. LOAD, SUB and STORE each make ONE further memory access for their data; JUMPNEG and HALT make none.

| Address | Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | LOAD 200 | ACC <- contents of address 200 |
| 101 | SUB 201 | ACC <- ACC - contents of address 201 |
| 102 | JUMPNEG 106 | If ACC < 0, continue at address 106 |
| 103 | LOAD 200 | ACC <- contents of 200 |
| 104 | STORE 202 | Contents of 202 <- ACC |
| 105 | HALT | Stop |
| 106 | LOAD 201 | ACC <- contents of 201 |
| 107 | STORE 202 | Contents of 202 <- ACC |
| 108 | HALT | Stop |

Before the run, address 200 holds 45, address 201 holds 60 and address 202 holds 0. Execution starts at 100.
stimuli.solution: 45 - 60 = -15 is negative, so the jump is taken: the instructions run are 100, 101, 102, 106, 107 and 108, and 60 is stored in 202. The program stores the larger of the two numbers. Memory accesses = 6 instruction fetches + 4 data accesses (LOAD, SUB, LOAD, STORE) = 10.

stimuli.title: Overnight batch jobs on an end-of-day server
stimuli.content:
A bank's end-of-day (EOD) server has one CPU and runs four batch jobs. Times are in minutes after the batch window opens. A SMALLER priority number means a HIGHER priority. A job's turnaround time = completion time - arrival time; its waiting time = turnaround time - burst time. Ignore context-switch time.

| Job | Task | Arrival time | CPU burst | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| J1 | Interest posting | 0 | 8 | 3 |
| J2 | ATM cash reconciliation | 1 | 4 | 1 |
| J3 | Statement generation | 2 | 9 | 4 |
| J4 | Loan EMI debit | 3 | 5 | 2 |
stimuli.solution: Non-preemptive priority: J1 runs 0-8 (only job present at 0), then J2 8-12, J4 12-17, J3 17-26; turnaround times 8, 11, 24 and 14, average 14.25 minutes. Preemptive priority: J1 0-1, J2 1-5, J4 5-10, J1 10-17, J3 17-26; waiting times J1 9, J2 0, J3 15, J4 2, average 6.5 minutes.

stimuli.title: DNS records seen by a branch PC
stimuli.content:
A branch technician looks up the bank's names with a DNS tool and gets these resource records (TTL in seconds; all records are class IN):

| Name | TTL | Type | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| netbanking.bank.example | 300 | CNAME | web.bank.example |
| web.bank.example | 300 | A | 203.0.113.25 |
| web.bank.example | 300 | AAAA | 2001:db8:10::25 |
| bank.example | 3600 | MX | 10 mail1.bank.example |
| bank.example | 3600 | MX | 20 mail2.bank.example |
| bank.example | 86400 | NS | ns1.bank.example |
| bank.example | 86400 | NS | ns2.bank.example |
| 25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa | 3600 | PTR | web.bank.example |
stimuli.solution: netbanking.bank.example is an alias of web.bank.example, whose IPv4 address is 203.0.113.25 (A record) and IPv6 address is 2001:db8:10::25 (AAAA record). Mail goes first to mail1 (MX preference 10, lower is preferred). ns1 and ns2 are the authoritative name servers of the zone. The PTR record under in-addr.arpa maps the IP address back to a name. TTL tells resolvers how many seconds they may cache each record.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A student simplified 120 − 40 ÷ 5 × 2 + 6 by first working out 120 − 40 and then going strictly from left to right. By how much was his answer less than the correct value?

solution.concept: Division and multiplication come before subtraction, working left to right
solution.why_others_wrong: 84 takes the correct value as 120 − 40 ÷ 10 + 6 = 122; 110 and 38 are the two values, not their difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What must be added to 2⅓ + 3⅚ to make the sum 7?

solution.concept: Add the whole numbers and the fractions separately, then subtract from 7
solution.why_others_wrong: ⅙ is the fractional part of the sum, not the shortfall; 1⅙ takes the sum as 5⅚, forgetting to carry 7/6 into the whole number; 1⅚ takes the sum as 5⅙.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the value of √(0.09 × 0.16 × 2.25)?

solution.why_others_wrong: 1.8 and 0.018 misplace the decimal point; 0.0324 is the product before taking the square root.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 9ˣ = 27ʸ and x + y = 5, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: Write both sides as powers of 3 and compare the indices
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 is the value of y (it comes from 3x = 2y); 2.5 assumes x = y; 4 gives y = 1, but 9⁴ ≠ 27.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = 7 − 4√3, what is the value of √x + 1/√x?

solution.why_others_wrong: 2√3 is 1/√x − √x; 14 is x + 1/x; √14 forgets the + 2 in (√x + 1/√x)² = x + 1/x + 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
[(0.1)² + (0.01)² + (0.009)²] ÷ [(0.01)² + (0.001)² + (0.0009)²] = ?

solution.concept: Each term of the numerator is 10 times the matching term of the denominator
solution.explanation: 0.1 = 10 × 0.01, 0.01 = 10 × 0.001 and 0.009 = 10 × 0.0009, so every square in the numerator is 10² = 100 times the matching square below. The quotient is 100.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 forgets that the terms are squared; 1,000 cubes the factor 10; 0.01 inverts the quotient.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If √x ÷ √441 = 0.02, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: √441 = 21; find √x first and then square it
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.42 is √x, not x; 1.764 and 0.01764 misplace the decimal point when squaring 0.42.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 + … + 1/1024 = ?

solution.concept: Each partial sum falls short of 1 by the last term added
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 is the sum of the endless series, not of these ten terms; 511/512 stops at 1/512; 1025/1024 adds the last term instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
∛(1 − 127/343) = ?

solution.concept: Combine into a single fraction first; then take the cube root of the numerator and the denominator
solution.why_others_wrong: 216/343 forgets the cube root; 36/49 is (6/7)²; 2/7 treats ∛(1 − a) as 1 − ∛a with ∛127 ≈ 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = (√5 + √3)/(√5 − √3) and y = (√5 − √3)/(√5 + √3), what is the value of x² + xy + y²?

solution.concept: Here xy = 1; find x + y and use x² + xy + y² = (x + y)² − xy
solution.why_others_wrong: 62 is x² + y² (leaving out xy); 64 is (x + y)²; 65 adds xy to (x + y)² instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Find the value of the endless product 2^(1/2) × 4^(1/4) × 8^(1/8) × 16^(1/16) × …

solution.concept: Write every factor as a power of 2: (2ⁿ)^(1/2ⁿ) = 2^(n/2ⁿ); then add the indices
solution.explanation: The product is 2 raised to S = 1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + 4/16 + …. Then S/2 = 1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + …, and S − S/2 = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … = 1. So S = 2 and the product is 2² = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 takes the sum of the indices as 1 (the series 1/2 + 1/4 + …); 2√2 takes it as 3/2; 8 takes it as 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
1 × 2 + 2 × 3 + 3 × 4 + … + 20 × 21 = ?

solution.explanation: Each term is k² + k, so the sum is (1² + … + 20²) + (1 + … + 20) = 2,870 + 210 = 3,080. The formula gives 20 × 21 × 22 ÷ 3 = 3,080 directly.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,870 adds only the squares; 3,542 includes one term too many (up to 21 × 22); 2,660 uses k(k − 1) in place of k(k + 1).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
45.02% of 1,599.6 ÷ 8.97 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round the percentage, the number and the divisor, then work left to right
solution.why_others_wrong: 90 divides 720 by 8; 72 divides by 10; 64 uses 36% instead of 45% (576 ÷ 9).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
√8.98 × √15.97 × √24.96 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Each number under a root is close to a perfect square
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 adds 9, 16 and 25 instead of multiplying their roots; 120 doubles the product; 45 takes √16 as 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
0.498 × 1,201.3 + 0.249 × 799.6 ≈ ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 750 takes ¼ of 800 as 150; 900 takes ¼ of 1,200 instead of 800 for the second part (600 + 300); 700 takes 0.249 as 1/8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of 640.2 + 39.97 ≈ 199.8

solution.concept: Subtract first, then find what percentage the remainder is of 640
solution.why_others_wrong: 31 forgets to subtract 40 (200 ÷ 640 ≈ 31%); 6.25 finds 40 as a percentage of 640; 35 adds 40 instead of subtracting it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(√? − 3.02) × 4.97 ≈ 75.03

solution.concept: Undo the steps in reverse order: ÷ 5, + 3, then square
solution.why_others_wrong: 289 = 17² and 361 = 19² come from adding 2 or 4 instead of 3; 225 = 15² forgets to add 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
4.98⁴ ÷ 24.97 + 3.02⁵ ÷ 8.99 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Write the powers of 5 and 3 and cancel with the divisors (25 = 5², 9 = 3²)

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(?% of 3,600.2 + 1/7 of 979.6) ÷ 8.02 ≈ 16.97 × 5.02

solution.concept: Multiply out the ÷ 8 first, take away the known part, then divide by 36 (1% of 3,600)
solution.why_others_wrong: 19 forgets to take away the 140 (680 ÷ 36); 23 adds 140 instead of subtracting it; 30 divides 540 by 18 instead of 36.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
∛? ≈ √1,155.8 + √4,227.1 − √8,460.2

solution.why_others_wrong: 512 = 8³ and 216 = 6³ come from misjudging one root by 1; 49 squares 7 instead of cubing it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
? ÷ 14.01 + 11.99 × 3.002 ≈ 4.002⁴ ÷ 3.998 − 8.998

solution.concept: Simplify the right side, subtract the product, then multiply by 14
solution.why_others_wrong: 238 and 294 are 17 × 14 and 21 × 14, from slips of 2 in the subtraction; 770 forgets to subtract 12 × 3 (55 × 14).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
40, 51, 64, 79, 96, ?

solution.concept: The differences are consecutive odd numbers: 11, 13, 15, 17, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 113 adds 17 again; 117 adds 21 and skips 19; 192 doubles 96.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, −2, 7, −20, 61, ?

solution.concept: Each term is −3 times the previous term, plus 1
solution.why_others_wrong: −183 forgets the + 1; 182 drops the minus sign; −122 multiplies by −2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 15, 23, ?

solution.concept: The differences are the Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … (each the sum of the two before)
solution.explanation: Differences: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. The next is 5 + 8 = 13, so the term is 23 + 13 = 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 31 adds 8 again; 38 adds the last two terms (15 + 23); 39 doubles the last difference (+16).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
7, 19, 37, 61, 91, ?

solution.concept: Each term is the difference of consecutive cubes: 2³ − 1³, 3³ − 2³, 4³ − 3³, …
solution.shortcut: Differences 12, 18, 24, 30 rise by 6; the next difference is 36.
solution.why_others_wrong: 125 is 5³ itself; 121 adds 30 again; 133 adds 42 and skips 36.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
2, 12, 30, 56, ?, 132

solution.concept: Each term is the product of two consecutive numbers: 1 × 2, 3 × 4, 5 × 6, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 72 = 8 × 9 and 110 = 10 × 11 shift the pairs by one; 81 = 9² uses only one factor.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 3, 14, 55, 174, ?

solution.concept: Each term is twice the previous term plus 1³, 2³, 3³, 4³, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 564 adds 6³ and skips 5³; 412 adds 4³ again; 522 triples 174 instead of doubling it and adding a cube.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 6, 15, 28, 55, 78, ?

solution.concept: The n-th term is n × (n-th prime): 1 × 2, 2 × 3, 3 × 5, 4 × 7, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 91 = 7 × 13 repeats the prime 13; 133 = 7 × 19 skips 17; 112 = 7 × 16 uses 16, which is not prime.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
12, 72, 240, 600, 1,260, ?

solution.concept: Each term is n² × (n² − 1) = n⁴ − n² for n = 2, 3, 4, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 2,401 is 7⁴ without subtracting 7²; 2,058 is 7³ × 6 (n³(n − 1)); 2,256 is 48 × 47, which shifts both factors down by one.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 4, 9, 25, 64, ?

solution.concept: The terms are squares of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …, where each base is the sum of the two bases before it
solution.explanation: Bases: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 (1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8). The next base is 5 + 8 = 13, so the term is 13² = 169.
solution.why_others_wrong: 121 = 11² and 144 = 12² use bases 8 + 3 and 8 + 4; 128 doubles 64 instead of squaring the next base.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 2, 3, 10, 39, 196, ?

solution.concept: From the third term on, add the two terms before and multiply by 1, 2, 3, 4, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 940 multiplies the sum by 4 again; 1,410 multiplies by 6; 235 adds the two terms but does not multiply.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
5, 12, 26, 47, 76, 110, 152

solution.why_others_wrong: 12, 47 and 152 fit; 110 − 35 = 75 confirms that 76 is wrong.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
5, 7, 11, 19, 35, 69, 131

solution.concept: Each term is twice the previous term minus 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 11, 35 and 131 fit; 131 confirms 67, since 69 × 2 − 3 = 135.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
7, 10, 17, 28, 44, 62, 85

solution.concept: The differences rise by 4 each time: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23
solution.why_others_wrong: 10, 28 and 62 fit; 62 − 19 = 43 confirms that 44 is wrong.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 5, 11, 29, 83, 245, 733

solution.concept: Each term is 3 times the previous term minus 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 11, 83 and 245 each equal 3 × (previous) − 4; only the last term breaks the rule.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
0, 14, 78, 252, 622, 1,290, 2,394

solution.concept: Each term is n⁴ − n for n = 1, 2, 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 14, 252 and 2,394 are 2⁴ − 2, 4⁴ − 4 and 7⁴ − 7; only 622 breaks the rule.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 4, 12, 30, 68, 148, 304

solution.concept: Add 1, 2, 3, 4, … to the term and then double

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 5, 14, 29, 86, 175, 518, 1,037

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for all their roots.
I. x² − 3x − 70 = 0
II. y² + 17y + 70 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 10)(x + 7) = 0, so x = 10 or −7. II: (y + 7)(y + 10) = 0, so y = −7 or −10. The smallest x (−7) equals the largest y (−7), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = −7; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The two quadratics below have large constant terms. Factorise them and pick the relation that is true for every pair of roots.
I. x² − 31x + 240 = 0
II. y² − 35y + 304 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each equation and look for a common root
solution.explanation: I: (x − 15)(x − 16) = 0, so x = 15 or 16. II: (y − 16)(y − 19) = 0, so y = 16 or 19. The largest x (16) equals the smallest y (16), and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 16; x > y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has one positive and one negative root. Solve I and II and compare x with y.
I. 3x² + 10x − 8 = 0
II. 2y² − 13y + 20 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.explanation: I: 3x² + 12x − 2x − 8 = (3x − 2)(x + 4) = 0, so x = 2/3 or −4. II: 2y² − 8y − 5y + 20 = (y − 4)(2y − 5) = 0, so y = 4 or 2.5. The largest x (0.67) is below the smallest y (2.5), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y reverse the comparison; every root of I is below every root of II.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The roots of both equations below are positive. Solve them and mark the relation between x and y.
I. 4x² − 21x + 27 = 0
II. 5y² − 13y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise by splitting the middle term
solution.explanation: I: 4x² − 12x − 9x + 27 = (4x − 9)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 3 or 2.25. II: 5y² − 10y − 3y + 6 = (5y − 3)(y − 2) = 0, so y = 2 or 0.6. The smallest x (2.25) exceeds the largest y (2), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail for every pair; no root is shared, so the relation is strict.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Both equations have negative fractional roots. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y, if any, that holds for all their roots.
I. 6x² + 23x + 20 = 0
II. 3y² + 11y + 10 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise and place all four roots on the number line
solution.explanation: I: 6x² + 15x + 8x + 20 = (2x + 5)(3x + 4) = 0, so x = −2.5 or −1.33. II: 3y² + 6y + 5y + 10 = (y + 2)(3y + 5) = 0, so y = −2 or −1.67. x = −2.5 is below both values of y, but x = −1.33 is above both. No relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = −1.33; x ≥ y fails for x = −2.5; x > y and x ≤ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair of roots.
I. 8x² − 26x + 15 = 0
II. 2y² − 11y + 15 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise both; a common root makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: 8x² − 20x − 6x + 15 = (2x − 5)(4x − 3) = 0, so x = 2.5 or 0.75. II: 2y² − 5y − 6y + 15 = (2y − 5)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 2.5 or 3. The largest x (2.5) equals the smallest y (2.5), and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 2.5; x > y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is linear with decimal coefficients and equation II is quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 0.6x − 1.5 = 0.35x + 0.5
II. y² − 22y + 117 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Collect the x-terms of I; factorise II
solution.explanation: I: 0.6x − 0.35x = 0.5 + 1.5, so 0.25x = 2 and x = 8. II: (y − 9)(y − 13) = 0, so y = 9 or 13. x = 8 is below both values of y, so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y would need x to be at least 9; solving I as 0.95x = 2 (adding the coefficients) is the usual slip.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has no constant term. Find all roots of I and II (do not divide by x) and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 4x = 0
II. y² + 5y + 4 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: x² − 4x = x(x − 4): x = 0 is also a root
solution.explanation: I: x(x − 4) = 0, so x = 0 or 4. II: (y + 1)(y + 4) = 0, so y = −1 or −4. The smallest x (0) exceeds the largest y (−1), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail for every pair, even if x = 0 is (wrongly) dropped by dividing by x.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The roots of both equations are fractions. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 9x² − 18x + 8 = 0
II. 10y² − 7y + 1 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.explanation: I: 9x² − 12x − 6x + 8 = (3x − 4)(3x − 2) = 0, so x = 4/3 or 2/3. II: 10y² − 5y − 2y + 1 = (2y − 1)(5y − 1) = 0, so y = 1/2 or 1/5. The smallest x (0.67) exceeds the largest y (0.5), so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail for every pair; no root is shared, so the relation is strict.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
The equations below have decimal coefficients. Solve them and choose the relation between x and y, if any.
I. x² − 1.3x + 0.4 = 0
II. y² − 1.1y + 0.28 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Find two numbers with the given sum and product (or multiply by 100 and factorise)
solution.explanation: I: the roots add to 1.3 and multiply to 0.4, so x = 0.8 or 0.5. II: the roots add to 1.1 and multiply to 0.28, so y = 0.7 or 0.4. x = 0.5 is less than y = 0.7 but more than y = 0.4. No relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for 0.5 and 0.7; x ≤ y fails for 0.8 and 0.7; x < y and x ≥ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option D: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is given as a square. Take both square roots, solve II, and compare x with y.
I. (x − 2)² = 9
II. y² − 15y + 50 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.explanation: I: x − 2 = ±3, so x = 5 or −1. II: (y − 5)(y − 10) = 0, so y = 5 or 10. x = 5 equals one value of y and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 5; x ≥ y fails for x = −1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is exponential. Find every real x and y and choose the relation between them.
I. 2^(2x) − 6 × 2ˣ + 8 = 0
II. y² − 5y + 6 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Put t = 2ˣ: equation I becomes a quadratic in t, and t must be positive
solution.explanation: I: t² − 6t + 8 = 0, so t = 2 or 4, that is 2ˣ = 2 or 2ˣ = 4, giving x = 1 or 2. II: (y − 2)(y − 3) = 0, so y = 2 or 3. The largest x (2) equals the smallest y (2), and every other pair has x < y. So x ≤ y.
steps: max x = 2 = min y ⇒ x ≤ y
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = y = 2; x ≥ y would follow only if the roots t = 2, 4 were mistaken for the values of x.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the LCM of 2³ × 3² × 5 and 2² × 3³ × 7?

solution.concept: The LCM takes every prime to its highest power in either number
solution.explanation: Highest powers: 2³, 3³, 5 and 7. LCM = 8 × 27 × 5 × 7 = 7,560.
solution.why_others_wrong: 36 = 2² × 3² is the HCF; 2,72,160 is the product of the two numbers (360 × 756); 1,260 uses the lower power of 2 and 3² instead of 3³.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the unit digit of 13²⁰²⁵ − 7²⁰²⁵?

solution.concept: Unit digits of powers of 3 and 7 repeat every 4; 13²⁰²⁵ is the larger number, so borrow when needed
solution.explanation: 2025 = 4 × 506 + 1, so 13²⁰²⁵ ends in 3 and 7²⁰²⁵ ends in 7. 13²⁰²⁵ is larger, so the difference ends in 13 − 7 = 6 (borrowing 10).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 uses the third place of the cycles (7 − 3); 0 uses the second place (9 − 9); 3 is the unit digit of 13²⁰²⁵ alone.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest five-digit number that is exactly divisible by 7, 11 and 13?

solution.concept: A number divisible by 7, 11 and 13 is a multiple of their LCM, 7 × 11 × 13 = 1,001
solution.explanation: Multiples of 1,001: …, 9,009, 10,010, …. 9,009 has four digits, so the smallest five-digit multiple is 10 × 1,001 = 10,010.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10,001 = 73 × 137 is not a multiple of 1,001; 9,009 has only four digits; 10,101 = 1,001 × 10 + 91 is not a multiple of 1,001 (though it is divisible by 7 and 13).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many positive integers less than 1,000 leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 4 and a remainder of 2 when divided by 5?

solution.concept: Find the smallest such number; the rest follow at intervals of LCM(4, 5) = 20
solution.explanation: Numbers leaving 2 on division by 5: 2, 7, 12, 17, … The first that leaves 1 on division by 4 is 17. So the numbers are 17, 37, 57, …, 997. Count = (997 − 17) ÷ 20 + 1 = 50.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49 forgets to count the first term; 200 counts the numbers that satisfy only the remainder-2 condition; 100 divides 1,000 by 10 instead of 20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A batter scores 84 runs off 60 balls. Her strike rate is the number of runs per 100 balls. What is her strike rate?

solution.why_others_wrong: 71.4 divides balls by runs; 124 adds 84 + 40 (the balls short of 100); 144 takes 84 ÷ 60 as 1.44.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Each month an employee puts 12% of her basic pay into her provident fund, and her employer adds an equal amount. In a year the total credited to her provident fund is ₹86,400. What is her monthly basic pay?

solution.concept: Each month 12% + 12% = 24% of the basic pay is credited
solution.explanation: Monthly credit = 86,400 ÷ 12 = ₹7,200. This is 24% of the basic pay, so basic = 7,200 ÷ 0.24 = ₹30,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹60,000 ignores the employer's equal share (12% only); ₹36,000 divides the yearly total by 2.4; ₹3,60,000 is the yearly basic pay, not the monthly.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sapling is 25 cm tall. Its height grows by 20% every month, each time on its height at the start of that month. How tall is it after 3 months?

solution.why_others_wrong: 40 cm adds 20% of 25 three times (simple growth of 60%); 36 cm stops after 2 months; 51.84 cm runs for 4 months.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of cooking oil rises by 25%, and a family's spending on oil rises by only 5%. As a result the family now buys 4 litres less oil each month. How many litres did it buy each month before the price rise?

solution.concept: Quantity = spending ÷ price, so the new quantity is 1.05 ÷ 1.25 = 0.84 of the old
solution.explanation: New quantity = 1.05/1.25 = 84% of the old, a fall of 16%. 16% of the old quantity = 4 litres, so the old quantity = 4 ÷ 0.16 = 25 litres.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 litres takes the fall as 20% (25 − 5); 16 litres is the 16% itself; 21 litres is the new quantity.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Two identical machines were bought at the same price. The first, bought 3 years ago, depreciates by 10% a year and is now worth ₹3,64,500. The second, bought 2 years ago, depreciates by 20% a year. What is the second machine worth now? (Each year's depreciation is on the value at the start of that year.)

solution.concept: Find the common purchase price from the first machine, then depreciate it for the second
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,91,600 applies 20% to ₹3,64,500 once; ₹3,00,000 uses simple depreciation (40% of ₹5,00,000); ₹2,33,280 depreciates ₹3,64,500 at 20% for 2 years.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A salesman can choose between two pay plans. Plan P: ₹6,000 a month plus 5% commission on the first ₹50,000 of sales and 4% on sales above that. Plan Q: ₹4,000 a month plus 6% commission on sales above ₹20,000. At what monthly sales do the two plans pay the same?

solution.concept: Write each plan's pay for sales S above ₹50,000 and equate
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,25,000 ignores Plan Q's ₹20,000 threshold (6,500 + 0.04S = 4,000 + 0.06S); ₹3,20,000 pays Plan P 5% on all sales; ₹1,60,000 pays Plan P 4% on all sales.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The sides of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5 and its perimeter is 84 cm. How long is the longest side?

solution.concept: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 parts
solution.explanation: One part = 84 ÷ 12 = 7 cm. The longest side = 5 × 7 = 35 cm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28 cm and 21 cm are the other two sides; 42 cm takes half the perimeter.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x : 15 :: 36 : 27, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: In a proportion, product of extremes = product of means: x × 27 = 15 × 36

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A's monthly salary is three-fifths of B's, and B earns ₹15,000 more than A. What is A's monthly salary?

solution.concept: The ₹15,000 gap is 2/5 of B's salary
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹37,500 is B's salary; ₹9,000 is 3/5 of ₹15,000; ₹25,000 takes the gap as 3/5 of B's salary.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of a teacher and a student are in the ratio 5 : 2. Three years ago the ratio was 3 : 1. How old was the teacher when the student was born?

solution.concept: Let the ages be 5k and 2k; the teacher's age at the student's birth is the age gap 3k
solution.explanation: (5k − 3) = 3(2k − 3) gives 5k − 3 = 6k − 9, so k = 6. Ages: teacher 30, student 12. The gap, 18 years, was the teacher's age when the student was born.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 and 12 are the present ages; 27 is the teacher's age three years ago.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a : b = 3 : 5, what is (7a − 2b) : (3a + 4b)?

solution.concept: Put a = 3k and b = 5k; k cancels
solution.explanation: 7a − 2b = 21k − 10k = 11k and 3a + 4b = 9k + 20k = 29k. The ratio is 11 : 29.
solution.why_others_wrong: 29 : 27 swaps a and b (a = 5, b = 3); 29 : 11 inverts the answer; 21 : 29 drops the − 2b.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A piggy bank holds ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins whose numbers are in the ratio 6 : 4 : 3. The ₹5 coins are worth ₹140 more than the ₹2 coins. What is the total value of the coins?

solution.concept: Take the numbers as 6k, 4k and 3k; their values are 6k, 8k and 15k rupees
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹460 leaves out the ₹1 coins; ₹290 and ₹1,160 use k = 10 and k = 40.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In an office the ratio of officers to clerks is 2 : 7. After 6 clerks are promoted to officers (no one joins or leaves), the ratio becomes 1 : 2. How many more clerks must now be promoted to make the numbers of officers and clerks equal?

solution.concept: Promotions move people between the groups; the total stays the same
solution.explanation: Let the numbers be 2k and 7k. (2k + 6) : (7k − 6) = 1 : 2 gives 4k + 12 = 7k − 6, so k = 6: 12 officers and 42 clerks, 54 in all. Now there are 18 officers and 36 clerks. Equal numbers means 27 each, so 9 more promotions.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 counts from the original 12 officers; 27 is the number in each group at the end; 6 repeats the first promotion.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Five years from now, Kabir will be three times as old as he was 15 years ago. How old is Kabir now?

solution.concept: Form one equation in Kabir's present age
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is (5 + 15) alone; 30 is his age 5 years from now; 35 solves k + 5 = 3k − 45 as 2k = 70.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of P and Q are in the ratio 5 : 6, and Q is 4 years older than P. How old will P be 7 years from now?

solution.concept: The age gap of 4 years is 6 − 5 = 1 part
solution.explanation: 1 part = 4 years, so P = 5 × 4 = 20 and Q = 24. Seven years from now P will be 27.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is P's present age; 31 is Q's age 7 years from now; 24 is Q's present age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Twelve years ago, Sita was four times as old as her daughter. Six years from now, their ages will add up to 76 years. What is Sita's present age?

solution.concept: Six years from now both are 6 years older, so the present sum is 76 − 12 = 64
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is the daughter's age; 50 is Sita's age six years from now; 32 is her age twelve years ago.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Six years from now the ages of X and Y will be in the ratio 7 : 5. X is 8 years older than Y. What is Y's present age?

solution.concept: The age gap does not change: 7 − 5 = 2 parts = 8 years
solution.explanation: 1 part = 4 years, so in six years X = 28 and Y = 20. Y's present age = 20 − 6 = 14.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 is Y's age six years from now; 22 is X's present age; 28 is X's age six years from now.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: In 2026, a child's age (in completed years) equals the sum of the digits of the year in which the child was born. How old is the child in 2026?

solution.concept: If the child was born in 20ab, the age is 26 − 10a − b and the digit sum is 2 + a + b
solution.explanation: For a birth year 20ab: 26 − 10a − b = 2 + a + b, so 11a + 2b = 24. The only digits that work are a = 2, b = 1: born in 2021, age 5 = 2 + 0 + 2 + 1. (A birth year in the 1900s would need 11a + 2b = 116, which no digits satisfy.)
solution.why_others_wrong: A child aged 7, 6 or 4 would be born in 2019, 2020 or 2022, with digit sums 12, 4 and 6, which do not match.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of 12, 18, 25, x and 30 is 22. What is x?

solution.explanation: Total = 22 × 5 = 110. The four known numbers add up to 85, so x = 110 − 85 = 25.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22 is the average itself; 30 takes the total as 115; 20 takes the known sum as 90.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average temperature from Monday to Thursday was 36°C and from Tuesday to Friday was 37°C. Friday's temperature was 9/8 of Monday's. What was Friday's temperature?

solution.concept: The two four-day totals differ only by Friday − Monday
solution.explanation: Friday − Monday = 4 × 37 − 4 × 36 = 4°C. With F = 9M/8, F − M = M/8 = 4, so M = 32°C and F = 36°C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32°C is Monday's temperature; 40°C takes F − M as 8; 37°C is an average, not Friday's reading.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of the 40 employees of a branch is 32 years. The average age of the men is 36 and that of the women is 26. How many women work there?

solution.why_others_wrong: 24 is the number of men; 20 assumes equal groups; 12 uses the ratio 7 : 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When a 34-year-old member of a team retires and is replaced by a 22-year-old, the average age of the team falls by 1.5 years. How many members does the team have?

solution.concept: The total falls by 34 − 22 = 12 years, spread over all the members
solution.explanation: Fall in total = 12 years = team size × 1.5. Team size = 12 ÷ 1.5 = 8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 is the fall in the total; 18 multiplies 12 by 1.5; 6 divides 12 by 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average of some numbers is 24. If the largest of them, 64, is removed, the average becomes 22. If instead only the smallest number is removed, the average becomes 25. What is the smallest number?

solution.concept: First find how many numbers there are from the first removal
solution.explanation: 24n − 64 = 22(n − 1) gives 2n = 42, so n = 21 and the total is 504. Removing the smallest: 504 − s = 25 × 20 = 500, so s = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 takes 20 numbers in all (480 − 25 × 19); 24 is the average itself; 9 takes the total as 509.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average weight of A, B and C is 60 kg. When D joins them, the average becomes 62 kg. Then E, who is 3 kg heavier than D, replaces A, and the average weight of B, C, D and E becomes 61 kg. What is A's weight?

solution.concept: Work with totals: A + B + C, then D, then B + C
solution.why_others_wrong: 65 kg takes E as 3 kg lighter than D; 71 kg and 68 kg are E's and D's weights.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bicycle bought for ₹3,600 is sold at a loss of 15%. What is the selling price?

solution.concept: Selling price = 85% of the cost price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹4,140 adds 15%; ₹540 is the loss itself; ₹3,130 divides 3,600 by 1.15.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Selling an article at its marked price gives a profit of 32%. Selling it at a discount of ₹96 on the marked price gives a profit of 20%. What is the marked price?

solution.concept: The ₹96 discount equals the drop in profit, 32% − 20% = 12% of the cost price
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹800 is the cost price; ₹960 is the selling price after the discount; ₹1,200 takes ₹96 as 8% of the marked price.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
