questions.question_text:
Four boxes P, Q, R and S have different weights. On a balance:
- P and Q together exactly balance R and S together.
- P and R together are heavier than Q and S together.
- P and S together are lighter than Q and R together.

Which box is the heaviest?

solution.concept: Add and subtract the balance relations
solution.explanation: Write P + Q = R + S (1), P + R > Q + S (2), P + S < Q + R (3). (2) − (1): R − Q > Q − R, so R > Q. (1) + (3): 2P + Q + S < 2R + Q + S, so R > P. From (1), R − P = Q − S, and R > P, so Q > S; also R > P and (2) + (1) give P > S. So R is heavier than P, Q and S.
steps: R > P > S (and Q > S) ⇒ R heaviest
solution.why_others_wrong: P and Q are each lighter than R; S is the lightest box.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who is the Coordinator?

solution.explanation: Kamini > Pratik > Naina > Lokesh occupy ranks 3–6, so Kamini is the Coordinator.
steps: Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Asst Teacher–English
solution.why_others_wrong: Pratik is the Senior Teacher, Oorja the Vice-Principal and Naina the Teacher.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which subject does Lokesh teach?

solution.explanation: Maths (Oorja), History (Madhav), Science (Pratik) and Music (Naina) are taken; Lokesh does not teach Art, so English.
steps: Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Asst Teacher–English
solution.why_others_wrong: Art is Kamini's subject, Maths Oorja's and History Madhav's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who teaches Maths?

solution.explanation: The Maths teacher is the Vice-Principal; Madhav is senior to Oorja, so Madhav is the Principal and Oorja the Vice-Principal who teaches Maths.
steps: Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Asst Teacher–English
solution.why_others_wrong: Madhav teaches History, Kamini Art and Pratik Science.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following person – post – subject combinations is correct?

solution.explanation: Naina is the Teacher and teaches Music.
steps: Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Asst Teacher–English
solution.why_others_wrong: Pratik is the Senior Teacher, Madhav the Principal and Kamini the Coordinator.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'X % Y & Z', how is Z related to X?

solution.concept: The wife of one's father is one's mother
solution.explanation: X is Y's daughter and Y is Z's husband, so Z is X's mother.
steps: X % Y: X is Y's daughter
Y & Z: Z is Y's wife ⇒ X's mother
solution.why_others_wrong: Z is a generation above X, so not her sister or daughter; nothing puts her two generations above.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'M ! N & O', how is O related to M?

solution.concept: A son's wife is a daughter-in-law
solution.explanation: M is N's father and N is O's husband, so O is the wife of M's son: M's daughter-in-law.
steps: M ! N: N is M's son (a husband is male)
N & O: O is N's wife ⇒ daughter-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: O is married into the family, not M's own daughter; M's wife is N's mother; O is a generation below M.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'R ! S % T', how is T related to R?

solution.explanation: R is S's father; S is T's daughter, so T is S's other parent, her mother. T is therefore R's wife.
steps: R ! S: R is S's father
S % T: T is S's parent ⇒ mother
Father and mother of S ⇒ T is R's wife
solution.why_others_wrong: S is the daughter; T and R are S's two parents, so T is neither R's sister nor his mother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Usha is the mother of Vinay. Vinay is the brother of Wamiqa, and Xavier is Wamiqa's husband. How is Usha related to Xavier?

solution.explanation: Vinay and Wamiqa are siblings, so Usha is Wamiqa's mother too. Xavier is Wamiqa's husband, so Usha is his mother-in-law.
steps: Usha = mother of Vinay and Wamiqa
solution.why_others_wrong: Xavier is not Usha's own son; she is a generation above him, so not his sister-in-law; an aunt is a parent's sister.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Deepak is the only son of Eshwar. Geeta is Deepak's sister, and Farida is Geeta's daughter. How is Deepak related to Farida?

solution.explanation: Deepak is the brother of Farida's mother Geeta, so he is Farida's (maternal) uncle.
solution.why_others_wrong: Farida's father is Geeta's husband; Deepak is a generation above Farida, so not her brother; her grandfather is Eshwar.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Hari is the husband of Ila. Ila's only son is Jai, and Jai's wife is Kiya. Lina is Kiya's daughter. How is Hari related to Lina?

solution.explanation: Jai is the son of Hari and Ila, and Lina is the daughter of Jai and his wife Kiya. Hari is Lina's father's father: her grandfather.
steps: Lina = Jai's daughter ⇒ Hari is her grandfather
solution.why_others_wrong: Lina's father is Jai; Hari is two generations above her; he is Kiya's father-in-law, not Lina's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Looking at the photograph of a woman, Kunal said, "Her husband's mother is the only sister of my father." How is the woman related to Kunal?

solution.concept: Collapse the phrase from the inside out
solution.explanation: The only sister of Kunal's father is Kunal's paternal aunt. Her son, the woman's husband, is Kunal's cousin, so the woman is the wife of Kunal's cousin.
solution.why_others_wrong: She is not a child of Kunal's parents; the aunt is her mother-in-law, not her; she is related to Kunal only by marriage, so not his own cousin.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Wife of his cousin

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

options.text: A is the son of D
A is the uncle of C
D is the husband of B

solution.explanation: A is B's brother; B is C's mother; C is D's daughter, so D is C's father and B's husband. So A is C's maternal uncle, D is B's husband and C is a girl — all true. A is B's brother, i.e. D's brother-in-law, not D's son.
steps: A @ B, B # C ⇒ A is C's maternal uncle
C $ D with B the mother ⇒ D is the father, B's husband
A is D's brother-in-law ⇒ 'son of D' is false
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three statements follow directly from the code.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A is the son of D

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Om is the father of Usha, and Tia is Usha's daughter. Usha's only sibling is Varun, and Wanda is Varun's wife. How is Wanda related to Tia?

solution.explanation: Varun is the brother of Tia's mother Usha, i.e. Tia's maternal uncle. Wanda, his wife, is Tia's aunt.
solution.why_others_wrong: Tia's mother is Usha; Wanda is Usha's sister-in-law, not Tia's; Tia's grandmother is Om's wife.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Qasim related to Pranav?

solution.explanation: Pranav's father Mehul is Naina's brother, and Qasim is Naina's husband, so Qasim is Pranav's uncle (paternal aunt's husband).
steps: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya
Qasim = husband of Pranav's father's sister ⇒ uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: Pranav's father is Mehul; Qasim's child Riya is Pranav's cousin; his grandfather is Kartik.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Leela related to Riya?

solution.explanation: Riya's mother is Naina (Qasim's wife), and Naina is Leela's daughter, so Leela is Riya's grandmother.
steps: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya
solution.why_others_wrong: Riya's mother is Naina; Leela is two generations above Riya; she is Qasim's mother-in-law, not Riya's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Ojasvi related to Naina?

solution.explanation: Ojasvi is married to Mehul, Naina's brother, so Ojasvi is Naina's sister-in-law.
steps: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya
solution.why_others_wrong: Ojasvi has different parents from Naina; she is in Naina's generation, so not her mother-in-law; cousins share grandparents.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Sahil is the only son-in-law of Rohan's paternal grandfather. Rohan's father has exactly one sibling, and every person mentioned has only one spouse. How is Sahil related to Rohan?

solution.concept: A son-in-law must be married to a daughter
solution.explanation: A son-in-law of Rohan's grandfather is married to one of the grandfather's daughters. The grandfather's children are Rohan's father and his only sibling, so that sibling is a daughter: Rohan's paternal aunt. Sahil is her husband, i.e. Rohan's uncle.
steps: Only sibling of Rohan's father ⇒ that daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: Rohan's father is a son of the grandfather, not a son-in-law; Sahil is a generation above Rohan, so not his brother-in-law or cousin.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Uncle (husband of his father's sister)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Test every option; the gender of P must be fixed
solution.explanation: In 'P ™ Q ® S', P is Q's daughter and Q is S's brother, so P is the daughter of S's brother: S's niece. In 'S ® Q © P', S is the brother of P's mother, but P's gender is unknown (nephew or niece). 'P ® Q ™ S' makes P S's son, and 'S © Q ® P' makes S P's mother.
steps: Option 1: daughter of S's brother ⇒ niece ✓
solution.why_others_wrong: The second does not fix P's gender; the third and fourth give son and mother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Early one morning, Kavya walked straight towards the sun. She then turned to her left and kept walking. In which direction was she walking then?

solution.concept: The morning sun is in the east
solution.explanation: Walking towards the morning sun means walking east. A left turn from east points north.
solution.why_others_wrong: South is a right turn from east; West is away from the sun; East ignores the turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between the depot and stop B, and in which direction is B from the depot?

solution.explanation: B is 6 km east and 8 km north of D: √(36 + 64) = 10 km, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '10 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '14 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is the end point F from the depot in a straight line, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement of the whole trip
solution.explanation: East: 6 − 12 + 10 = 4 km; north: 8 − 5 = 3 km. √(16 + 9) = 5 km, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: '5 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '5 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '7 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is stop C with respect to stop F?

solution.explanation: C (−6, 8) − F (4, 3) = (−10, 5): west and north, so C is north-west of F.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is F's direction from C; North-East misreads C as east of F; West ignores the 5 km north component.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which stop is nearest to the depot in a straight line?

solution.explanation: Distances from D: A 6 km, B 10 km, C 10 km, E √45 ≈ 6.7 km, F 5 km. F is nearest.
solution.why_others_wrong: A is 6 km, E about 6.7 km and B 10 km away.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A girl is facing south-east. She turns 135° anticlockwise three times in a row. Which direction is she facing now?

solution.explanation: Three turns of 135° make 405° anticlockwise, which is a full circle plus 45°. 45° anticlockwise from south-east is east.
solution.why_others_wrong: North and South-West come from stopping after one or two turns; South turns the last 45° the other way.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: At about 5 pm, Anil and Bhanu were walking straight towards each other on a road. Anil's shadow fell directly behind him. In which direction was Bhanu walking?

solution.explanation: At 5 pm the sun is in the west, so shadows point east. Anil's shadow was behind him, so Anil was walking west, towards the sun. Bhanu, walking towards Anil, was walking east.
steps: Shadow behind Anil ⇒ Anil walks west
Bhanu walks the opposite way ⇒ east
solution.why_others_wrong: West is Anil's direction; North and South are at right angles to the road's direction.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Sneha cycles 7 km towards the north, turns right and cycles 5 km, turns left and cycles 4 km, turns right and cycles 9 km, and then turns right again and cycles 11 km. How far is she from her starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: North and south legs may cancel
solution.explanation: North 7 + 4 = 11, then south 11: the north–south parts cancel. East 5 + 9 = 14 km. She is 14 km due east of the start.
steps: Turn right from north ⇒ east: 5 km → (5, 7)
Turn left from east ⇒ north: 4 km → (5, 11)
Turn right from north ⇒ east: 9 km → (14, 11)
Turn right from east ⇒ south: 11 km → (14, 0)
solution.why_others_wrong: West mixes up the right turns; 36 km adds every leg; 11 km, South is only the last leg.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which point lies exactly midway between K and J?

solution.concept: Drop M onto the line KJ
solution.explanation: M = (5, 5) is the midpoint of KL. N is 5 m south of M, i.e. (5, 0), which is exactly halfway along KJ from (0, 0) to (10, 0).
solution.why_others_wrong: M is 5 m north of KJ, O is 2 m west of K's north–south line, and L is 10 m north of J.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between K and M, and in which direction is M from K?

solution.explanation: M is the midpoint of KL, and L is 10 m east and 10 m north of K, so M is 5 m east and 5 m north of K: 5√2 m, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 m, North ignores the east part; 10 m takes the full side length; South-West is K's direction from M.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is L from O, and in which direction is L from O?

solution.explanation: O = (−2, 5) and L = (10, 10): L is 12 m east and 5 m north of O, √(144 + 25) = 13 m, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West is O's direction from L; 17 m adds the two parts; 12 m, East ignores the north part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, SALT is written as WEPX. How is CORN written in that code language?

solution.concept: Every letter moves forward by the same number of places
solution.explanation: S→W, A→E, L→P, T→X: every letter moves 4 places forward. C→G, O→S, R→V, N→R: GSVR.
solution.why_others_wrong: YKNJ moves the letters back; GSVQ moves N only 3 places; HTWS moves every letter 5 places.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 5274 is written as 6385 and 3916 is written as 4027. How is 8093 written in that code?

steps: Each digit +1, keeping only the units digit
solution.why_others_wrong: 7982 subtracts 1; 9105 adds 2 to the last digit; 3909 reverses the number and changes nothing else.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, LEMON is written as LMKCJ and GRAPE is written as CNYPE. How is MELON written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse, then move each letter back
solution.explanation: LEMON reversed is NOMEL; each letter moved 2 places back: L M K C J. GRAPE → EPARG → C N Y P E. MELON → NOLEM → L M J C K.
solution.why_others_wrong: KCJML shifts without reversing; PQNGO moves the letters forward; LMJCL moves the last letter back only once.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 4815 is written as 3366 and 2967 is written as 8547. How is 7302 written in that code?

solution.concept: Swap the halves, then +2 and −2 alternately
solution.explanation: 4815: the two halves are interchanged → 1548; then the 1st and 3rd digits get +2 and the 2nd and 4th get −2: 3 3 6 6. 2967 → 6729 → 8 5 4 7. 7302 → 0273 → 0+2 = 2, 2−2 = 0, 7+2 = 9, 3−2 = 1: 2091.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9180 applies the +2/−2 without swapping; 0273 only swaps; 2093 adds 2 to the last digit.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is 'BRIDGE' written in this code?

solution.explanation: BRIDGE: last letter E, 6 letters, B + 2 = D, giving E6D. Six is even, so the code is reversed: D6E.
solution.why_others_wrong: E6D forgets the reversal; D6F reverses but shifts the wrong letter; E6B does not shift B.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is 'STAMP' written in this code?

solution.explanation: STAMP: last letter P, 5 letters, S + 2 = U. Five is odd, so the code stays P5U.
solution.why_others_wrong: U5P reverses an odd-length code; P5T moves S only one place; R5U shifts the last letter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words is written as 'K7R' in this code?

solution.explanation: K7R is not reversed only if the word has an odd number of letters: 7 letters, ending in K, with first letter R − 2 = P. PADLOCK fits. SHAMROCK → U8K, PARK → R4K, PLUCK → K5R.
steps: Last letter K, first letter P, 7 letters ⇒ PADLOCK
solution.why_others_wrong: SHAMROCK has 8 letters and starts with S; PARK has 4 letters (code reversed); PLUCK has 5.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 3rd to the left of the 6th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Convert a right-end position, then move left
solution.explanation: The 6th from the right is the 12th from the left (F). Three places to its left is the 9th element: K.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many numbers in the arrangement are immediately followed by a letter?

solution.concept: Look at the right neighbour of every number
solution.explanation: Numbers and their right neighbours: 3 %, 8 A, 5 K, 1 F, 7 I, 2 Y. Followed by a letter: 8 A, 5 K, 1 F, 7 I, 2 Y — 5.
steps: Keep those with a letter on the right

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the numbers are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 7th from the left end?

solution.explanation: Without numbers: W % H A @ K £ F I # Y. The 7th from the left is £.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Which term should replace the question mark in the series?

C3, F6, I9, L12, ?

solution.concept: The number is the letter's position
solution.explanation: The letters move 3 places forward each time (C, F, I, L, O) and each number is its letter's position (3, 6, 9, 12, 15). The next term is O15.
solution.why_others_wrong: O14 and N15 break the link between the letter and its position; P15 moves the letter 4 places.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

T % A 6 # E @ 9 U $ R I ¥ 4 O & B

How many vowels in the arrangement are immediately followed by a symbol?

solution.concept: Look at the right neighbour of every vowel
solution.explanation: Vowels and their right neighbours: A 6, E @, U $, I ¥, O &. Followed by a symbol: E @, U $, I ¥, O & — 4.
steps: Vowels: A, E, U, I, O
Keep those with a symbol on the right

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If every letter in the arrangement is replaced by the letter that comes immediately after it in the English alphabet, how many vowels will the new arrangement contain?

solution.concept: Only letters just before a vowel become vowels
solution.explanation: A letter becomes a vowel only if it is D, H, N, T or Z (→ E, I, O, U, A). Letters of the arrangement: M, D, U, S, E, K, V, A, Z, H, O. Of these, D, Z, H become vowels — 3.
steps: Letters before vowels: D, H, N, T, Z

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many symbols are there between the 2nd vowel from the left end and the 3rd number from the right end?

solution.explanation: 2nd vowel from the left: E (10th). 3rd number from the right: 3 (16th). Between them: # K 9 V £. Symbols: #, £ — 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 7th to the right of the element that lies exactly midway between the 2nd and the 12th elements from the left end?

solution.explanation: Midway between the 2nd and 12th is the (2 + 12) ÷ 2 = 7th element (©). Seven places to its right is the 14th element: V.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the symbols are removed and then the first twelve of the remaining elements are written in reverse order, which element will be 7th from the right end?

solution.concept: Delete, then reverse a block, then count
solution.explanation: Without symbols (23 elements): 5 Q E 8 J 2 I N 7 T 4 O P 3 G A 9 L 6 K U 1 R. Reversing the first twelve: O 4 T 7 N I 2 J 8 E Q 5 P 3 G A 9 L 6 K U 1 R. The 7th from the right is 9.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters in the arrangement are immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by an even number?

solution.explanation: Letters with a symbol on the left: @ E 8, # T 4, & O P, £ G A, ¥ L 6, * U 1. Of these, followed by an even number: @ E 8, # T 4, ¥ L 6 — 3.
steps: Find letters with a symbol on the left
Keep those with an even number on the right

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the consonants are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 4th to the right of the 5th element from the left end?

solution.explanation: Without consonants: 5 @ E 8 % 2 I 7 # 4 & O 3 £ A 9 ¥ 6 * U 1. The 5th element is %; four places to its right is the 9th: #.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the difference between the sum of the numbers that are immediately preceded by a vowel and the sum of the numbers that are immediately followed by a vowel?

solution.explanation: Preceded by a vowel: 8, 9, 1 (sum 18). Followed by a vowel: 2 (sum 2). Difference: 16.
steps: Numbers with a vowel on the left
Numbers with a vowel on the right
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options are one of the two sums alone, or their total.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many times does a number stand exactly two places to the right of a vowel (with one element in between)?

solution.concept: Check the element two places to the right of every vowel
solution.explanation: Each vowel with the element two places to its right: E … J, I … 7, O … 3, A … ¥, U … R. Numbers there: I N 7, O P 3 — 2.
steps: Vowels: E, I, O, A, U
Look two places to the right of each

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters of the word have a position in the English alphabet that is a prime number?

solution.explanation: Positions: R 18, E 5, P 16, U 21, B 2, L 12, I 9, C 3, A 1, N 14, S 19. Prime positions: E (5), B (2), C (3), S (19) — 4.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which letter is 3rd to the right of the letter that lies exactly midway between the 1st and 9th letters of the word?

solution.explanation: Midway between the 1st and 9th letters is the 5th letter, B. Three places to its right is the 8th letter: C.
solution.why_others_wrong: I is 7th and A 9th; L is only one place to the right of B.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many pairs of letters in the word have as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting both forward and backward)?

solution.concept: Compare the gap in the word with the gap in the alphabet
solution.explanation: Pairs found: RP, RU, EB — 3 in all.
steps: Positions: R 18, E 5, P 16, U 21, B 2, L 12, I 9, C 3, A 1, N 14, S 19
A pair qualifies when |word gap| = |alphabet gap|

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which letter is as many places to the right of P in the English alphabet as K is to the right of D?

solution.concept: Find the gap, then apply it
solution.explanation: K (11) is 7 places to the right of D (4). Seven places to the right of P (16) is the 23rd letter: W.
solution.why_others_wrong: V and X are 6 and 8 places from P; I is 7 places to the left of P.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the words MANAGE, MANAGER, MANAGING and MANAGEMENT are arranged in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary, which word will be third?

solution.concept: A shorter word that is the start of a longer one comes first
solution.explanation: MANAGE comes first, being the beginning of the others. MANAGEMENT and MANAGER both start with MANAGE; their next letters are M and R, so MANAGEMENT comes before MANAGER. MANAGING (I after MANAG, and I > E) comes last. Third: MANAGER.
solution.why_others_wrong: MANAGEMENT is second, MANAGING fourth and MANAGE first.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the vowels are removed from the English alphabet, which letter will be 12th from the right end of the remaining letters?

solution.explanation: Without A, E, I, O, U, 21 letters remain. The 12th from the right is the 21 − 12 + 1 = 10th from the left: B C D F G H J K L M — M.
steps: 12th from the right = 10th from the left
solution.why_others_wrong: L and N are one place off; O is a vowel and has been removed.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Twenty-six children sit in a row facing north. Tia is 12th from the right end. How many children sit to the left of Tia?

solution.concept: Children to the left = position from the left − 1
solution.explanation: Tia is 26 − 12 + 1 = 15th from the left, so 14 children sit to her left.
solution.why_others_wrong: Fifteen is her position from the left; Eleven counts the children to her right; Thirteen subtracts one too many.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five students Arya, Bela, Chhavi, Dina and Esha scored different marks in a test.
- Arya scored more than Bela but less than Chhavi.
- Dina scored less than Bela.
- Esha scored more than Chhavi.

Who scored the lowest marks?

solution.explanation: Esha > Chhavi > Arya > Bela > Dina. Dina scored the lowest.

solution.explanation: Q is heavier than R alone, so R is the lightest and Q second lightest. S is lighter than T alone, so T is the heaviest and S second heaviest. P is left for the middle place.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Twenty-five students with roll numbers 1 to 25 sit in a row facing north, in order of roll number from the left end. All the students with odd roll numbers leave the row, and the others do not move relative to one another. What is the position of roll number 14 from the right end in the new row?

solution.concept: Count only the students who remain
solution.explanation: The remaining students are roll numbers 2, 4, …, 24 — twelve students. Roll number 14 is 7th of them from the left, so it is 12 − 7 + 1 = 6th from the right.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7th is its place from the left; 12th is the number of students left; 5th forgets the + 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Eighteen lamp posts stand in a straight row, 25 m apart from one another. What is the distance between the 3rd post from the left end and the 4th post from the right end?

solution.concept: Distance = number of gaps × gap length
solution.explanation: The 4th post from the right is 18 − 4 + 1 = 15th from the left. From the 3rd to the 15th post there are 15 − 3 = 12 gaps of 25 m: 300 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 325 m counts 13 gaps (posts, not spaces); 275 m counts 11; 350 m counts 14.

solution.explanation: Arun 8th, Bela 14th, Chetan 11th, Dinesh 16th from the left; Dinesh is 4th from the right, so the row has 16 + 4 − 1 = 19 persons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 and 20 drop or double the − 1; 22 places Dinesh on the wrong side of Chetan.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons sit between Arun and Dinesh?

solution.explanation: Arun is 8th and Dinesh 16th from the left: 16 − 8 − 1 = 7 persons sit between them.
solution.why_others_wrong: Eight forgets the − 1; Six subtracts one too many; Nine counts both ends.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is Chetan's position from the right end?

solution.concept: Position from the other end = total − position + 1
solution.explanation: Chetan is 11th from the left in a row of 19: 19 − 11 + 1 = 9th from the right.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11th is his place from the left; 8th and 10th misuse the + 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Esha sits exactly midway between Arun and Dinesh. Who sits immediately to the left of Esha?

solution.concept: Midway = average of the two positions
solution.explanation: Arun is 8th and Dinesh 16th, so Esha is (8 + 16) ÷ 2 = 12th from the left. The 11th place, immediately to her left, is Chetan's.
solution.why_others_wrong: Bela is two places to Esha's right; Arun and Dinesh are the two ends of the stretch.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step. In each step it makes two moves: (1) among the numbers not yet arranged, it takes the one that leaves the smallest remainder when divided by 7, replaces it by the quotient of that division, and places the quotient at the left end, immediately to the right of the quotients already placed there; (2) among the words not yet arranged, it takes the one that comes last in alphabetical order, writes it in capital letters, and places it at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already placed there. All other elements keep their order.

Input: pearl 45 coral 30 amber 61 topaz 20

What is the sum of all the numbers in Step III?

solution.concept: Track which numbers are still unchanged in the step
solution.explanation: Remainders on division by 7: 30 → 2, 45 → 3, 61 → 5, 20 → 6, so the numbers are taken in the order 30, 45, 61, 20 and become 4, 6, 8, 2. Words from last alphabetically: topaz, pearl, coral, amber. Step I: 4 pearl 45 coral amber 61 20 TOPAZ. Step II: 4 6 coral amber 61 20 PEARL TOPAZ. Step III: 4 6 8 amber 20 CORAL PEARL TOPAZ. Sum of the numbers in Step III = 38.
steps: Step I: 4 pearl 45 coral amber 61 20 TOPAZ
Step II: 4 6 coral amber 61 20 PEARL TOPAZ
Step III: 4 6 8 amber 20 CORAL PEARL TOPAZ

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Assumptions:
I. There are dustbins in the park.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.explanation: Visitors are told to use the dustbins, so the notice takes for granted that dustbins are there (I). A reminder to keep the park clean is put up only if littering is expected otherwise (II).
steps: Instruction to use dustbins ⇒ dustbins exist: I
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one of two things the notice rests on.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit

questions.question_text:

steps: Promise tied to a target ⇒ the target is reachable: I
'Not work at all' is an extreme claim ⇒ II not implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:

Statement: A bank has cut its home-loan interest rate by 0.25 percentage point to attract new borrowers.

Assumptions:
I. Some borrowers choose a lender partly on the basis of the interest rate it charges.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: A rate cut can attract borrowers only if borrowers care about the rate (I). The bank may expect rivals to follow; its move does not depend on their keeping their rates unchanged (II).
steps: Rate cut to attract borrowers ⇒ borrowers compare rates: I
Rivals' reaction is not part of the plan ⇒ II not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both assume something about other banks that the decision does not need; Neither ignores why a rate cut would attract anyone.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Assumptions:

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.explanation: Schools are closed because heavy rain could endanger children on their way (II). Acting on a forecast as a precaution does not require being certain that it will come true, so I ('certainly') is not assumed.
steps: Closure for safety ⇒ rain can make travel unsafe: II
Precaution, not certainty ⇒ I not implicit

questions.question_text:

Targeting girls does not imply boys need no transport ⇒ II not implicit

solution.explanation: Allowing work from home makes sense only if at least some work can be done from home (II). The notice allows work on Fridays, from home; it does not assume that all the week's work is done by Thursday (I).

Friday is still a working day ⇒ I not implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Each of the five trainees in a batch passed at least one of two tests, Hindi and English. Exactly three of them passed the Hindi test, and exactly three passed the English test.

Conclusions:
I. At least one trainee passed both tests.
II. Exactly one trainee passed both tests.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Passing counts add up to 3 + 3 = 6 for 5 trainees who each passed at least one test, so exactly 6 − 5 = 1 trainee was counted twice, that is, passed both. 'Exactly one' (II) and therefore 'at least one' (I) both follow.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one of two consequences of the same count.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

The café is located near a college

solution.concept: Weaken: give another reason for the rise
solution.explanation: A half-price offer in the same week could explain the jump in sales by itself, so the rise does not show that customers like the new menu.
steps: Weakener: 50% discount in the same week
solution.why_others_wrong: The kind of dishes, the location and who designed the menu do not explain a sudden one-week rise.
solution.final_answer: Option C: During that first week, the café gave a 50% discount on every item to celebrate the new menu

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Many small traders in a town are losing sales because they accept only cash, while more and more customers want to pay digitally.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Ask customers to carry more cash
Help the traders open free QR-code payment accounts with their banks and show them how to use them
Ban digital payments in the town
Close the shops that accept only cash

solution.concept: Enable the traders rather than restrict the customers
solution.explanation: Traders lose sales because they cannot accept digital payments. Helping them start accepting such payments removes the problem.
solution.why_others_wrong: Banning digital payments or telling customers to carry cash goes against what customers want; closing shops punishes the traders.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Help the traders open free QR-code payment accounts with their banks and show them how to use them

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A museum gives free entry to children under 12 years of age and to people over 60. All other visitors pay ₹50 each. On Sunday, a family visited the museum: a grandmother aged 65, two parents aged 38 and 36, and two children aged 12 and 8.

Which of the following can be inferred?

options.text: The family paid ₹150 in all for entry
The family paid ₹200 in all for entry
The family paid ₹100 in all for entry
The family paid ₹250 in all for entry

solution.explanation: The grandmother (over 60) and the 8-year-old (under 12) enter free. The two parents and the 12-year-old (who is not under 12) pay ₹50 each: ₹150.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹100 treats the 12-year-old as under 12; ₹200 charges the grandmother or the younger child; ₹250 charges everyone.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The family paid ₹150 in all for entry

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Countries with more mobile phones per person have higher average incomes. So giving free mobile phones to families in the state's poorest districts will raise their incomes.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Several companies sell mobile phones in the state
Most people in the poorest districts work in farming
Mobile phones have become cheaper in recent years
A trial last year that gave free phones to 10,000 families in two of the poorest districts found no change in their incomes after a year, compared with similar families who did not get phones

solution.concept: Weaken: direct evidence against the predicted effect
solution.explanation: The argument predicts that free phones will raise incomes. A controlled trial in the same kind of districts found no effect, which directly undercuts the prediction drawn from a country-level link.
solution.why_others_wrong: Cheaper phones, the main occupation and the number of sellers do not show whether phones raise incomes.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A trial last year that gave free phones to 10,000 families in two of the poorest districts found no change in their incomes after a year, compared with similar families who did not get phones

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The hospital's new rule that doctors must wash their hands before examining each patient is the reason infections among its patients fell by 30% this year.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: The hospital made no other change this year in its cleaning, staffing or kinds of patients, and similar hospitals without the rule saw no fall in infections
Doctors at the hospital agreed with the new rule
Hand-washing takes doctors less than a minute

solution.explanation: If nothing else changed at the hospital and comparable hospitals without the rule saw no fall, the new rule is the most likely reason for the drop in infections.
steps: Strengthener: no other change; no fall elsewhere
solution.why_others_wrong: The time hand-washing takes, the hospital's size and doctors' agreement do not link the rule to the fall.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The hospital made no other change this year in its cleaning, staffing or kinds of patients, and similar hospitals without the rule saw no fall in infections

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: Five lectures — on Economics, History, Law, Maths and Physics — are held one after another on a day. Law is held immediately after History. Maths is the third lecture. Physics is held at some time before Economics.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Physics is held immediately before Economics

solution.concept: Find every arrangement, then pick what holds in all
solution.explanation: History–Law must take places 1–2 or 4–5 (Maths is 3rd). If they are 1–2, Physics and Economics are 4th and 5th; if they are 4–5, Physics and Economics are 1st and 2nd. In both cases Physics comes immediately before Economics.
steps: Case 1: History, Law, Maths, Physics, Economics
Case 2: Physics, Economics, Maths, History, Law
Common to both: Physics just before Economics
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other options holds in only one of the two possible orders.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Physics is held immediately before Economics

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: A survey found that the city's buses run almost empty between 11 am and 4 pm but are badly overcrowded during the morning and evening peak hours.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Raise fares sharply during peak hours to keep people off the buses
Shift some buses from the afternoon schedule to the peak hours, and offer lower fares in the afternoon
Buy enough new buses to double the fleet at once
Stop all bus services between 11 am and 4 pm

solution.concept: Match supply to demand at low cost
solution.explanation: Buses are idle in the afternoon and short at peak hours. Moving buses to the peak hours uses the existing fleet better, and cheaper afternoon fares can draw some travellers away from the peaks.
steps: Problem: mismatch between bus supply and demand
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping afternoon buses strands those who travel then; doubling the fleet is costly and leaves more empty buses; sharp peak fares penalise people who must travel at those hours.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Shift some buses from the afternoon schedule to the peak hours, and offer lower fares in the afternoon

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Patients who choose Dr Mehta for knee surgery recover faster than the patients of the other knee surgeons at the hospital. So Dr Mehta is the hospital's best knee surgeon.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Dr Mehta's patients pay the same fees as other patients
Dr Mehta has worked at the hospital for ten years
Dr Mehta operates mostly on young athletes with minor injuries, while the other surgeons treat most of the elderly patients with severe knee damage
The hospital has four knee surgeons

solution.concept: Weaken: the groups being compared differ
solution.explanation: Young patients with minor injuries recover faster whoever operates on them. If Dr Mehta's patients are mostly such cases, their faster recovery does not show that he is the best surgeon.
steps: Evidence: faster recovery of Dr Mehta's patients
Weakener: his patients are easier cases
solution.why_others_wrong: Years of service, the number of surgeons and fees do not explain the difference in recovery.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Dr Mehta operates mostly on young athletes with minor injuries, while the other surgeons treat most of the elderly patients with severe knee damage

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: In a class, the average mark of the 20 boys is 60, and the average mark of the 30 girls is 70. There are no other students in the class.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: The average mark of the whole class is 65
Every girl scored more than every boy
At least one girl scored more than 70
The average mark of the whole class is 66

solution.concept: A combined average is weighted by group size
solution.explanation: Total marks = 20 × 60 + 30 × 70 = 1,200 + 2,100 = 3,300 for 50 students: average 66.
solution.why_others_wrong: 65 averages the two averages without weighting; every girl could have scored exactly 70; averages say nothing about every individual.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The average mark of the whole class is 66

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: An audit found that the city's government hospitals often run out of essential medicines because each hospital places its own orders late and in small quantities.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Ask patients to bring their own medicines
Stop giving free medicines at the hospitals
Set up a central system that tracks every hospital's stock and places orders automatically before stocks run low
Order a five-year stock of every medicine at once

solution.concept: Fix the ordering process that causes the shortage
solution.explanation: Shortages come from late, small orders by each hospital. Central tracking with automatic reordering keeps stocks up without the waste of huge one-time purchases.
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping free medicines or shifting the burden to patients defeats the purpose of the hospitals; a five-year stock would expire and waste money.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Set up a central system that tracks every hospital's stock and places orders automatically before stocks run low

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what does the thyroid gland use iodine for?

options.text: To make hormones that control growth and brain development
To help the stomach digest crops grown in hilly areas
To protect the neck from damp air and heat
To remove salt that the body does not need

solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The thyroid gland in the neck uses iodine to make hormones that control growth and the development of the brain.'
steps: Read what it uses iodine for
Hormones for growth and the brain
solution.why_others_wrong: Removing extra salt, guarding against damp and heat, and digesting crops are never given as the gland's work; damp air and heat are mentioned only as causes of iodine loss from stored salt.
solution.final_answer: Option A: To make hormones that control growth and brain development

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, is iodine deficiency common in hilly and flood-prone areas?

options.text: People in these areas do not like the taste of salt.
Rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil.
Salt cannot be carried to these areas during the rains.
The water in these areas destroys iodine in the body.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: in such areas 'rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil', so crops, and the people who eat them, get little iodine.
steps: Cause: iodine washed out of the soil
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage never says these people dislike salt, that salt cannot reach them, or that their water destroys iodine in the body.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Rain and rivers have washed much of the iodine out of the soil.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT given in the passage as a reason why salt was chosen to carry iodine?

options.text: Rich and poor alike consume it.
People eat it in roughly similar amounts.
Adding iodine to it costs very little.
It keeps its iodine for years even if left open.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every reason the passage gives
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 gives three reasons: rich and poor eat salt, in roughly similar amounts, and iodising it costs only a few paise per kilogram. Paragraph 5 says the opposite of the last statement: iodine escapes from salt that is stored carelessly.
steps: Rich and poor consume it: stated
Keeps iodine when left open: contradicted in paragraph 5
solution.why_others_wrong: Eating by rich and poor alike, similar amounts and low cost are all stated in paragraph 4, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It keeps its iodine for years even if left open.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'norm' as used in the passage ('iodised salt became the norm in most households')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: norm = what is usual or standard
solution.explanation: Over the decades iodised salt came to be used in most homes; it became the ordinary, expected thing, i.e. 'the usual practice'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Something found in most households is not 'a rare luxury'. No law is mentioned, so 'a strict rule' goes too far. The passage praises iodised salt, so 'a costly mistake' contradicts it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why does the passage advise keeping salt away from the stove?

options.text: Salt near the stove attracts insects.
The stove makes the salt taste bitter.
Salt near the stove is easily spilt into food.
Heat causes the iodine in the salt to escape.

solution.concept: Inference: linking the advice to the reason given earlier
solution.explanation: Paragraph 5 says that damp air, heat and sunlight cause iodine to escape, so a packet left near the stove loses its value. The advice in the last paragraph follows from this.
steps: Advice: keep salt away from the stove
Earlier reason: heat makes iodine escape
solution.why_others_wrong: Insects, taste and spilling are never mentioned; the only reason the passage gives is the loss of iodine.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Heat causes the iodine in the salt to escape.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: How Salt Is Made from Sea Water
Why Doctors Tell Us to Eat Less Salt
A Small Addition with a Big Benefit

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage explains why the body needs iodine, why salt was chosen to carry it, and how households can keep its benefit. A tiny addition to salt protects health: 'A Small Addition with a Big Benefit'.
steps: Paras 1-3: iodine and the harm its lack causes
solution.why_others_wrong: How salt is made is never described. Himalayan villages appear in one sentence only. The passage is not about eating less salt.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A Small Addition with a Big Benefit

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a reason why money in bank accounts goes unclaimed?

options.text: Some balances are too small to seem worth claiming.
Banks refuse to let customers close their old accounts.
People open new accounts in new towns without closing the old ones.
The family of a dead account holder does not know the account exists.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every reason the passage gives
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives three reasons: people move and open new accounts, small balances seem trivial, and families do not know about a dead relative's account. Nothing is said about banks refusing to close accounts.
steps: Moving without closing old accounts: stated
Family unaware after a death: stated
solution.why_others_wrong: Moving towns, trivial balances and unaware families are all named in paragraph 2, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Banks refuse to let customers close their old accounts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what happens to a deposit that remains unclaimed for ten years?

options.text: The bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.
The government spends it on new branches in villages.
The money is divided among the bank's other customers.
The bank adds it to its own profits for that year.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'If the deposit remains unclaimed for ten years, the bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.'
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says banks do not keep the money, so it is not added to profits. Spending on new branches and sharing among other customers are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The bank transfers it to a fund maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What can be understood from the passage about money that has been moved to the Reserve Bank's fund?

options.text: The owner or the legal heirs can still claim it, even years later.
It can never be returned once it has been moved.
It can be returned only if it is claimed within a month.
Only the Reserve Bank can decide whom to give it to.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says, right after describing the transfer, that 'The money still belongs to the depositor' and that the bank must pay it back if the owner or heirs come forward 'even many years later'.
steps: 'The money still belongs to the depositor'
Can be claimed 'even many years later'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Never returned' and 'only within a month' contradict 'even many years later'. The passage says the bank must pay the rightful owner, not that the Reserve Bank chooses whom to pay.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The owner or the legal heirs can still claim it, even years later.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'trivial' as used in the passage ('Small balances seem too trivial to bother about')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: trivial = of little importance
solution.explanation: People do not bother about small balances because the amounts seem too small to matter, i.e. 'unimportant'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A small balance is not 'dangerous'. 'Valuable' is the opposite of the sense. 'Complicated' does not explain why people would ignore a small sum.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how does registering a nominee help the family?

options.text: The bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork.
The account can never become inactive after a nominee is named.
The bank pays the family a higher rate of interest on the deposit.
The family no longer has to pay any tax on the money.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 5: 'Where a nominee is registered, the bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork.'
steps: Read what happens where one is registered
solution.why_others_wrong: Higher interest, freedom from tax and accounts that never become inactive are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The bank can usually settle the claim quickly and with far less paperwork.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best states the main purpose of the passage?

options.text: To describe how the Reserve Bank of India invests the money it receives
To criticise banks for hiding unclaimed money from their customers
To explain why bank deposits go unclaimed and how families can avoid the problem
To persuade people to keep their savings at home instead of in banks

solution.concept: Main purpose: what the passage as a whole sets out to do
solution.explanation: The passage describes how money becomes unclaimed, what banks do with it, why claiming it is hard, and how nomination, the search website and a list of accounts can prevent the problem. It explains and advises.
steps: Paras 3-4: what happens to it; claims are tiring
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says banks do not keep the money and must pay it back, so it does not accuse them. It never advises keeping savings at home. How the Reserve Bank invests the fund is not discussed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: To explain why bank deposits go unclaimed and how families can avoid the problem

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what does a forecast of 'a seventy per cent chance of rain' actually mean?

options.text: Rain is certain, and it will be heavier than on an ordinary day.
Rain will fall over about seventy per cent of the forecast area.
Rain will fall for about seventy per cent of the hours in the day.
At any spot in the area there is a seven-in-ten chance of some measurable rain.

solution.concept: Locating the stated definition and rejecting the common misreadings
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'at any given spot in the forecast area, there is a seven-in-ten chance of at least some measurable rain during the period.'
steps: Paragraph 2: 'None of these readings is correct'
Correct meaning: seven-in-ten chance at any spot
solution.why_others_wrong: Seventy per cent of the day, seventy per cent of the area and a promise of rain are exactly the misreadings that paragraph 2 rejects.
solution.final_answer: Option D: At any spot in the area there is a seven-in-ten chance of some measurable rain.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, do forecasters run their computer models many times?

options.text: Their starting measurements are never perfect, so they test many slightly different starts.
Computers often break down, so each run has to be repeated to get any result at all.
Each run covers only one town, so many runs are needed to cover a whole country.
People do not trust a single run, so repeated runs are made to persuade the public.

solution.concept: Inference: the reason stated in the same paragraph
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: the atmosphere is so sensitive that 'a tiny error in today's measurements can grow into a large error'. Forecasters 'therefore' run the models many times from slightly different conditions, and the share of runs that give rain sets the chance.
steps: 'Therefore': many runs from slightly different starts
Share of rainy runs → chance of rain
solution.why_others_wrong: Breakdowns, one-town coverage and persuading the public are never mentioned; the passage links repeated runs to the growth of small errors.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Their starting measurements are never perfect, so they test many slightly different starts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Four forecasters each predicted 'a seventy per cent chance of rain' on 40 days. Going by the test described in the passage, whose record shows that he or she is well calibrated?

options.text: The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 28 of the 40 days
The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 40 of the 40 days
The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 12 of the 40 days
The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 20 of the 40 days

solution.concept: Applying the calibration test: the share of rainy days should match the forecast figure
solution.explanation: A well-calibrated forecaster's seventy per cent days should turn out rainy about seventy per cent of the time. Seventy per cent of 40 days = 28 days, so the record '28 of the 40 days' passes the test.
steps: Test: share of rainy days ≈ forecast figure
solution.why_others_wrong: Rain on all 40 days (100%) means the figure was too low, 12 of 40 is 30% and 20 of 40 is 50%; none of these matches seventy per cent. Rain on every day may feel like success, but the passage judges the match between the figure and the outcome.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The one for whose forecasts rain fell on 28 of the 40 days

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'sensitive' as used in the passage ('The atmosphere is so sensitive that a tiny error ... can grow into a large error')?

options.text: likely to be hurt by criticism

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: one word, several senses; the clause after 'so ... that' fixes the sense
solution.explanation: The atmosphere is called sensitive because a tiny difference in the starting measurements can produce a large difference later. In this sense, 'sensitive' means easily affected by small changes.
steps: 'so sensitive that a tiny error can grow'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hurt by criticism' and 'kept secret' are other senses of 'sensitive' that do not suit the atmosphere. 'Able to detect faint sounds' describes an instrument or an ear, not the weather.
solution.final_answer: Option A: easily affected by small changes

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why might the family planning a wedding and the farmer in the last paragraph act differently on the same forecast?

options.text: Rain would ruin the wedding, while for the farmer it would only waste one spraying.
The farmer wants his crop to be washed by the rain before he sprays it.
The family trusts weather forecasts, while the farmer does not believe them at all.
The family receives a different forecast from the one the farmer receives.

solution.concept: Inference: decisions depend on the cost of being caught by rain, not on the forecast alone
solution.explanation: For the family, rain would be 'a disaster', so even a thirty per cent chance justifies a tent. For the farmer, a shower would only wash off the spray, so he can wait for a day when the chance is very low. The cost of each mistake differs.
steps: Wedding: rain = disaster → act even at 30%
Farmer: rain wastes the spray → spray only when the chance is low
Same forecast, different costs → different decisions
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says both act on 'the same forecast', so a different forecast or distrust is not the reason. The farmer wants to avoid rain washing off the spray, not to have the crop washed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Rain would ruin the wedding, while for the farmer it would only waste one spraying.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Reading the Odds in a Weather Forecast

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through every paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage explains what a percentage chance of rain means, where it comes from, how forecasters should be judged and how people can use it. Its subject is understanding the probability in a forecast.
solution.why_others_wrong: The monsoon is never discussed. The wedding is one example in the last paragraph. Computers are mentioned only as tools for running models, not as replacing weather stations.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Reading the Odds in a Weather Forecast

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What did the study of students' final-year theses described in the passage find?

options.text: Students who gave worst-case estimates always finished on time.
The students' estimates were accurate, but their teachers' were not.
Most students finished well before the dates they had first estimated.
On average, they finished later than their own estimate for things going badly.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'On average, they took longer than even their worst-case estimate.'
steps: Longer than even the worst case
solution.why_others_wrong: Finishing early, always finishing on time and accurate estimates all contradict the finding; teachers' estimates are not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: On average, they finished later than their own estimate for things going badly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what does taking the 'inside view' of a task involve?

options.text: Adding a fixed margin of extra time to every estimate one makes
Asking how long similar projects carried out by others actually took
Imagining one's own planned steps working out more or less as expected
Discussing the plan with colleagues before deciding on a date

solution.concept: Understanding a term defined in the passage
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'we picture the particular steps it requires and imagine them going roughly as intended. This is called taking the "inside view".'
steps: It is defined by the sentence before it
Picturing one's own steps going to plan
solution.why_others_wrong: Checking how long similar projects took is the 'outside view' of paragraph 5. Adding a margin and consulting colleagues are not what the passage calls the inside view.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Imagining one's own planned steps working out more or less as expected

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, are unplanned events such as an illness or a delayed supplier so damaging to estimates?

options.text: Each of them is very likely to happen on every single day of a project.
Any one of them is improbable, but on a long job a few are bound to occur.
Planners include them in their plans, which makes the plans too long.
They happen only on large public projects, which planners cannot control.

solution.explanation: The passage says each such event 'is unlikely on its own, but over a long project it is almost certain that some of them will happen'. Because the inside view leaves them out, the estimate is too short.
steps: Unplanned events are left out of the plan
Each is unlikely, but together they are near-certain
So estimates that ignore them are too short
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage gives everyday examples, so they are not limited to public projects. It calls each event unlikely, not likely every day. The problem is that planners leave such events out, not that they include them.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Any one of them is improbable, but on a long job a few are bound to occur.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'routinely' as used in the passage ('new airports routinely open years after their promised dates')?

options.text: deliberately, in order to save money
regularly, as a matter of course

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: routinely = as a normal, regular occurrence
solution.explanation: The passage says large projects show 'the same pattern', so late openings are the normal state of affairs: they happen regularly, as a matter of course.
steps: Context: 'the same pattern on a grander scale'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rarely' is the opposite of the sense. Nothing suggests the delays are sudden or deliberate; the passage treats them as a common pattern.
solution.final_answer: Option D: regularly, as a matter of course

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of the 'outside view' as the passage describes it?

options.text: A builder checks how long the last ten school buildings in the district really took before quoting a date.
A builder lists every step of the new building and adds up the time each step should take.
A builder ignores his past delays because each had a special cause, such as early rains.
A builder promises an early date because his workers are more skilled than those of his rivals.

solution.concept: Applying a concept: the outside view starts from the record of similar projects
solution.explanation: Paragraph 5: the planner 'first asks how long similar projects actually took'. Checking the actual time taken by ten similar school buildings is exactly this.
steps: Outside view: start from how long similar projects took
Ten past school buildings = similar projects
solution.why_others_wrong: Listing the steps is the inside view. Trusting one's own workers' skill also starts from the details of the present case. Explaining away past delays as special cases is the error described in paragraph 4.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A builder checks how long the last ten school buildings in the district really took before quoting a date.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author suggest in the last paragraph?

options.text: One should never try to estimate how long one's own work will take.
Picturing one's own task as someone else's may give a truer estimate.
Colleagues' tasks always take longer to finish than one's own tasks.
People should ask their colleagues to do their own work for them.

solution.concept: Inference: the conclusion the author draws
solution.explanation: When we judge others' tasks we think of their past record (the outside view), not their plan. So imagining our own task as someone else's may push us to use the record too: 'The best forecast ... may come from imagining that it belongs to someone else.'
steps: Others' tasks → we think of their record
Own task → we think of our plan
So treat one's own task as another's
solution.why_others_wrong: The author suggests imagining, not handing the work to colleagues. Nothing says colleagues' tasks take longer. The author wants better estimates, not no estimates.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Picturing one's own task as someone else's may give a truer estimate.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What did the flight instructor conclude from his experience?

options.text: Praise led to carelessness, while shouting pushed pilots to greater effort.
Praise and criticism had no effect at all on how pilots landed.
Trainee pilots needed more hours of practice before flying alone.
Pilots landed better on calm days than on windy ones.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Praise, he concluded, made pilots careless, and criticism made them try harder.'
solution.why_others_wrong: That praise and criticism had no effect is the psychologist's explanation, not the instructor's belief. Wind and practice hours are not part of his conclusion.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Praise led to carelessness, while shouting pushed pilots to greater effort.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, was the instructor misled?

options.text: His praise and criticism came only after extreme landings, so the usual drift back to normal looked like their effect.
His trainees practised in very different weather, so their landings could not be compared.
He remembered the rough landings more clearly than the smooth ones, so he misjudged his trainees.
He praised the trainees too often, so they stopped paying attention to anything he said.

solution.concept: Inference: identifying the cause of a mistaken conclusion
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'his words always came at the extremes ... so the natural movement back towards the average looked like the effect of his words.' Extreme landings are partly luck, so the next one tends to be more ordinary whatever he says.
steps: Feedback only after the best and worst landings
Next landing drifts back to normal anyway
The drift was mistaken for the effect of the feedback
solution.why_others_wrong: Praising too often contradicts 'praised only after the best landings'. Selective memory and weather differences are not the explanation the passage gives.
solution.final_answer: Option A: His praise and criticism came only after extreme landings, so the usual drift back to normal looked like their effect.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best example of regression to the mean as the passage describes it?

options.text: A batsman scores exactly his average of 40 in every one of his twenty innings.
A batsman whose average is 40 scores a career-best 180, and then scores 45 in his next innings.
A batsman scores less and less every season as an old knee injury slowly gets worse.
A batsman who practises harder every season raises his average from 30 to 45 over five years.

solution.concept: Applying a concept: an extreme result followed by one closer to the usual level
solution.explanation: A career-best 180 is an extreme result, helped by luck as well as skill. The next score, 45, falls back close to his normal average of 40, without any change in ability. That is regression to the mean.
steps: Extreme result: 180 against an average of 40
No change in ability needed → regression to the mean
solution.why_others_wrong: Steady improvement through practice and a steady decline through injury are real changes in ability, not a drift back after an extreme. Scoring exactly 40 every time shows no extreme result at all.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A batsman whose average is 40 scores a career-best 180, and then scores 45 in his next innings.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author imply about the city that installed speed cameras at its most dangerous junctions?

options.text: Accidents at those junctions will certainly rise again once the cameras are removed.
The city chose the junctions wrongly, because last year's figures were false.
The cameras were useless and the money should have been spent elsewhere.
A fall in accidents there does not, by itself, show how much the cameras helped.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says accidents will 'probably' fall 'partly because last year's figures were unusually high'. Paragraph 5 adds that this does not mean cameras do not work, only that a before-and-after comparison cannot tell us; comparable junctions without cameras are needed.
steps: Junctions chosen at an extreme year
Need a comparison group to measure the real effect
solution.why_others_wrong: The author says plainly that this does not mean cameras do not work. Nothing predicts what happens when cameras are removed. Last year's figures were unusually high, not false.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A fall in accidents there does not, by itself, show how much the cameras helped.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: As used in the passage ('luck does not repeat on demand'), the phrase 'on demand' means

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: on demand = as soon as or whenever it is asked for
solution.explanation: Good luck helped the smooth landing, but the trainee cannot call it up again whenever he wants it; luck does not come back 'on demand'.
steps: It cannot be produced again at will
solution.why_others_wrong: 'At a high price' and 'under a legal order' are senses linked to demand in trade and law, not here. 'After a long delay' says nothing about luck being available at will.
solution.final_answer: Option B: whenever it is wanted

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?

solution.concept: Tone: how the author treats the subject
solution.explanation: The author explains a statistical pattern with examples and warns readers not to trust simple before-and-after comparisons. That is explanatory and cautionary.
steps: Explains: luck, extremes, regression to the mean
solution.why_others_wrong: The author does not attack the instructor or anyone else, so the tone is not angry. The subject is treated seriously, not as a joke, and there is no longing for the past.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why do most of the positive results in the example come from healthy people?

options.text: Most people who take the test have already been told by a doctor that they are ill.
The disease often disappears on its own between the test and the result.
Healthy people so outnumber sick ones that a small error rate among them yields many false alarms.
The test is much better at detecting the disease in healthy people than in sick ones.

solution.concept: Inference: the base-rate reasoning in paragraph 3
solution.explanation: There are 99,900 healthy people and only 100 sick ones. Flagging just 5 in 100 healthy people gives 4,995 false alarms, far more than the 99 true cases. Paragraph 3 states this reason.
steps: 5% of 99,900 = 4,995 false alarms vs 99 true cases
Rarity of the disease → most positives are false
solution.why_others_wrong: The test detects 99 of every 100 sick people; it does not 'detect the disease' in healthy people better. Prior diagnosis and recovery between test and result are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Healthy people so outnumber sick ones that a small error rate among them yields many false alarms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Suppose the same test (detecting 99 of every 100 sick people and wrongly flagging 5 of every 100 healthy people) were used for a disease that affects 1 person in every 100. Using the method of the passage, roughly what share of the people who test positive would actually be ill?

solution.concept: Applying the passage's method (count people, not percentages) to a new base rate
solution.explanation: Out of 1,00,000 people, 1,000 are ill and the test flags 990 of them. Of the 99,000 healthy people, 5 in 100 = 4,950 are flagged. Positives = 990 + 4,950 = 5,940, of whom 990 are ill: 990/5,940 = 1/6.
solution.shortcut: Positives ≈ 990 true + 4,950 false; 990 is one sixth of 5,940
solution.why_others_wrong: 'About 99 in 100' and 'about 95 in 100' confuse the test's accuracy with the chance that a positive person is ill, the very error the passage warns against. 'About 1 in 50' is the passage's own answer for the rarer disease, before the base rate was changed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the author, how should a first positive result from such a screening test be treated?

options.text: As proof that the person certainly has the disease and needs treatment
As a sign that the screening test should be stopped for everyone
As a meaningless result, since the test cannot be trusted at all
As a reason for a second, more precise test rather than as a diagnosis

solution.concept: Inference: the author's conclusion in paragraph 4
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'the first result should be treated as a reason for further checks, not as a diagnosis', since it raises the chance of illness nearly twenty-fold and justifies 'a second, more precise test'.
steps: Positive result raises the chance nearly twenty-fold
But the chance is still under 2 in 100
solution.why_others_wrong: Treating the result as proof is the mistake the passage corrects. Calling it meaningless or stopping screening contradicts 'This does not make screening useless'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: As a reason for a second, more precise test rather than as a diagnosis

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'outweigh' as used in the passage ('can outweigh the benefit to the few who are truly ill')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: outweigh = be greater or more important than
solution.explanation: The author explains why doctors are cautious: the harm done to many wrongly flagged healthy people can be greater than the good done to the few sick ones. To 'outweigh' is to be greater than.
steps: Two things compared: harm to many vs benefit to few
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Be equal to' would give doctors no reason for caution. 'Be hidden by' and 'be paid for by' do not express a comparison of size.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the effect of a healthy habit on illness
solution.explanation: The passage praises handwashing as a way 'to stay healthy'. A healthy habit stops illnesses from happening: it can 'prevent' them.
